entries.title: Expand Smart Streets program citywide to enhance safety
entries.summary: <p>On Friday, less than a week after yet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/10/04/cyclist-fatally-hit-driver-east-garfield-park" >another cyclist’s death</a> over the weekend, the City Council’s <a class="Link" href="https://occprodstoragev1.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/meetingattachmentspublic/57db25a7-6e4d-40ac-9843-e8ad10c8a4bb.pdf" target="_blank" >Committee on Pedestrian and Traffic Safety</a> will have an opportunity to expand one of Chicago’s most promising tools for changing dangerous driving behavior — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/11/04/smart-streets-bus-bike-lane-ticket" >Smart Streets</a> program.</p><p>I like that the Smart Streets program is designed specifically to be about changing behavior, not money. People receive warnings first. This is to tell people: “We haven’t been caring about this, but we’re going to now.” Blocking a bike lane, parking at a bus stop or double parking with the flashers on “just to run in real quick” is not going to be something that's allowed anymore.</p><p>And it works. The city’s own data shows that 84% of drivers who received a zero-dollar warning did not go on to receive a fine. And 64% of drivers who received one ticket did not reoffend.</p><p>The pilot has demonstrated that this approach can change behavior. We should build on that success and make Smart Streets permanent citywide.</p><p><i>Cyrus Dowlatshahi, Humboldt Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-000000" name="module-000000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Establish term limits in Highland Park </h3><p>In less than a month, Highland Park residents will be asked to consider a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cityhpil.com/government/city_departments/city_managers_office/city_clerk/term_limits.php" target="_blank" >referendum </a>on whether term limits should be imposed on those seeking to run for mayor or the City Council.  Term limits have become a lightning rod of sorts for the electorate, not only on a local level, but for those serving nationally in Congress and the Supreme Court.  </p><p>Certainly there are pros and cons to imposing such limits, but as a 50-year resident of Highland Park, I can say from experience that local politicians who serve, or want to continue to serve, for lengthy periods do so by imperiling progress for the community with outdated notions and policies that once were effective but wane with time. These politicians become "stale."  It is time for a change, and Highland Park residents will have an opportunity to become part of a vanguard with some other municipalities in Lake, DeKalb, Cook and Will counties —including Lake Forest and Wilmette that neighbor Highland Park — by voting for such limits.</p><p><i>Miles Zaremski, Highland Park</i> </p><h3>Toilet talk</h3><p>Oui, oui to public toilets!</p><p>I couldn't agree more with Sun-Times columnist Neil Steinberg that providing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/04/public-toilet-chicago-bathroom-desert-paris-london-tourism-steinberg" >public restrooms</a> is a goal worth working toward in Chicago. I am someone who has often found myself in the undignified position of panicking while looking for a restroom. Public facilities would provide locals and visitors alike with dignity while exploring our city.</p><p><i>Robert Scheffel, North Center</i><br></p>

entries.title: Orthodox church modeled after 15th century monastery heads toward landmark status
entries.summary: <p>St. Simeon Mirotočivi Serbian Orthodox Church is easy to miss for most Chicagoans, owing to the fact that it's tucked away in the far southeast corner of the city — closer to Hammond, Indiana, than say, State and Madison.</p><p>However, those who have seen the church, at 3737 E. 114th St., are unlikely to forget it: a magnificent pile of Byzantine Revival architecture with its crucifix-topped towers and unique two-tone brickwork with an eye-opening array of arches, horizontal stripes and checkerboard patterns.</p><p>The church, which is located in the East Side neighborhood, is likely to get more attention soon. That’s because the edifice is on the road toward receiving city landmark status.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Planning and Development’s Historic Preservation Division recommended St. Simeon and its accompanying Serbian Hall for preliminary landmark status.</p><p>It was before the Commission on Chicago Landmarks on Thursday as part of a brief confirmation that the designation would align with the city's planning goals for the area. The commission could vote on the designation at next month's meeting.</p><p>The congregation supports the designation, landmarks officials said.</p><p>Landmark status would be a great win for the community and the Far Southeast Side, a part of town better known for surviving the 1970s and 1980s crash of the steel industry than for good architecture.</p><p>And if any church deserves it, it's St. Simeon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6b0000" name="image-6b0000"></a> <picture But put the two buildings side-by-side, and you'd hardly guess one is more than 500 years older than the other.</p><p>"The two buildings are separated by five centuries and 5,000 miles," the planning department's architectural historian Matt Crawford told the landmarks commission, when the preliminary designation was introduced last month. they were going to be able to build their own church in their style," she said. entries.title: To protect immigrant students, a Chicago-area college told Flock to remove its cameras. The company refused.
entries.summary: <p>When Elgin Community College hired Flock Safety to install six surveillance cameras in April 2025, President Peggy Heinrich thought they would “enhance the safety and security of students.”</p><p>The company’s automatic license plate readers use artificial intelligence to track the registration, model and details like dents and bumper stickers of every passing vehicle. They were supposed to help locate stolen cars and missing people.</p><p>But Heinrich started to wonder if the cameras were actually making students less safe after seeing news reports that data captured by Flock cameras in Illinois had been <a class="Link" href="https://www.nprillinois.org/illinois/2025-08-27/hundreds-of-police-departments-use-camera-company-accused-of-breaking-state-law" target="_blank" ><u>shared with U.S. Customs and Border Protection</u>.</a> Then in September 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement <a class="Link" href="https://elgin.edu/news/ecc-in-the-news/2025/reported-ice-activity-on-campus.php" target="_blank" ><u>detained an Elgin Community College student</u></a> in a campus parking lot.</p><p>More than half of students at the far west suburban Chicago campus identify as Latino. Heinrich said enrollment dipped. Students were afraid to come to class. College officials decided the cameras had to go.</p><p>“We're just doing everything we can here to be sure this feels like a safe place for our students to come,” Heinrich said. “We want them to come here and to be able to focus on learning.”</p><p>As concerns about Flock and other makers of automatic license plate readers continue to emerge, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/17/five-public-universities-in-illinois-use-controversial-flock-cameras-to-surveil-campus" target="_blank" ><u>students and educators across Illinois</u></a> are calling on college leaders to terminate their contracts with the company. They say the surveillance technology violates student privacy and endangers immigrant students and student activists who’ve been targeted by the Trump administration.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A Flock camera near the entrance to Joliet Junior College’s main campus. Students have to pass at least one of the college’s seven Flock cameras on their way to class there.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lisa Kurian Philip/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Public records obtained by surveillance researcher Torin Monahan and WBEZ show that data captured by Flock cameras at other Illinois public campuses, including <a class="Link" href="https://dataverse.unc.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.15139/S3/FDPBPJ" target="_blank" ><u>Joliet Junior College</u></a>, the University of Illinois Chicago and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, was searched dozens of times last year in connection with immigration enforcement. In some cases, federal immigration authorities directly accessed colleges’ data. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/news/2025/august-25-2025-giannoulias-audit-finds-license-plate-reader-company-in-violation-of-state-law.html" target="_blank" ><u>The Illinois Secretary of State</u></a> also found that U.S. Customs and Border Protection searched Illinois Flock data last year in violation of state law.</p><p>Heinrich said her staff audited the campus’ Flock data and found no evidence to suggest it had been accessed by federal immigration agents. Still, college officials asked Flock to remove the surveillance cameras “out of an abundance of caution for our students,” Heinrich said.</p><p>But getting the cameras taken down was not as simple as it sounds, especially because Flock retains ownership of the company’s equipment. Flock responded to Elgin Community College’s request with silence — and even resistance.</p><p>Flock Safety did not respond to WBEZ’s request for comment. <a class="Link" href="https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/does-flock-share-data-with-ice" target="_blank" ><u>The company has said</u></a> federal agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, can no longer access local Flock data unless law enforcement agencies grant access.</p><p>Surveillance experts say the company is financially incentivized to have as many cameras gathering data as possible even in places that no longer want them, because potential clients are looking for the surveillance network with the greatest reach.</p><p>“You get to access even more cameras throughout the country,” said Monahan, a professor at the University of North Carolina Chapel Hill.</p><p>Elgin Community College staff notified Flock in October 2025 that they wanted to cancel their contract and have the cameras taken down. Within a day, Heinrich said, Flock rejected the request and refused to uninstall the equipment on the basis that the company had not breached their agreement.</p><p>College officials reached out again in December 2025 and said they would pay for the remaining five months of the contract — they just wanted the cameras taken down.</p><p>“We never received a response back from Flock,” Heinrich said.</p><p>That’s when things got weird. Heinrich said Elgin Community College staff began to cover the cameras using black trash bags and zip ties so that they would not be able to capture footage. But workers in an unmarked vehicle, which Heinrich assumed belonged to Flock, repeatedly removed the coverings.</p><p>“We were kind of in a back and forth for a bit where we’d cover, and then when they'd come to service, they'd remove,” Heinrich said. “Then we'd cover and then they'd remove.”</p><p>This strange dance continued, Heinrich said, until Elgin Community College’s contract with Flock expired in April this year and the company uninstalled the cameras for good.</p><h3><b>Flock cameras can undermine efforts to make students feel welcome </b></h3><p>But public records show Flock’s license plate readers are still installed at several other colleges across the state, including at five of the state’s 12 public universities and at four community colleges.</p><p>That’s the case at southwest suburban Joliet Junior College. At the main campus entrance, which is bordered on one side by cornfields, students like Lui Rodriguez have to pass at least one of the college’s seven Flock cameras to get to class.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Joliet Junior College student Lui Rodriguez says the college staff do a lot to make students feel like they belong on campus. So he was shocked to learn the college contracts with Flock and that federal immigration agents have accessed data captured by cameras on campus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lisa Kurian Philip/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A third of students who attend Joliet Junior College, including Rodriguez, identify as Latino. The 26-year-old said the staff goes to great lengths to make students feel a sense of belonging. Rodriguez has even baked cookies with the dean of students to raise funds for the student group Latinos Unidos.</p><p>“The staff here care about the students,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>So Rodriguez was shocked when he found out that Joliet Junior College contracts with Flock — and that <u>public records show</u> data captured by cameras on campus was directly accessed by federal immigration agents last year.</p><p>“It's kind of like a backstab to the students,” Rodriguez said. “I wish more people knew about it.”</p><p>Katie Smith, a spokesperson for Joliet Junior College, said college leaders and campus police proactively review who has access to their Flock data and would take any misuse of this information seriously. The college’s contract with Flock is up for renewal in July 2027.</p><p>“The College remains committed to fostering a welcoming and inclusive environment for all students and staff while balancing its responsibility to provide a safe campus environment,” Smith said in a written statement. “The safety of our students and the broader campus community is paramount.”</p><p>But Rodriguez said those reassurances, and the Flock cameras, do not make him feel safer on campus.</p><p>“We’re being surveilled and our information can be used to track us down and detain us,” Rodriguez said. “That’s not conducive to education and learning.”</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: What’s your NITA dream project? Experts weigh in as new agency directing CTA, Metra, Pace plans budget
entries.summary: <p>Ever dream of a project to improve the city's trains and buses?</p><p>Maybe it's a specific bus lane. Or a new or extended L line. Or a Metra route.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/10/nita-northern-illinois-transit-authority-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >Northern Illinois Transit Authority</a> is finalizing its 2027 budget. As the new agency in charge of the CTA, Metra and Pace, NITA is seeking public input to fulfill its goal of transforming public transit into something everyone wants to use.</p><p>The Sun-Times wants to hear how you — our readers — want NITA to spend its nearly $1.5 billion in extra cash.</p><p>Send your recommendations to <a class="Link" href="mailto:dstruett@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >dstruett@suntimes.com</a> or fill out the form below. We plan to publish some of them in the near future.</p><p>Meanwhile, here are the NITA dream projects of some transit experts:</p><h3>More housing near transit hubs</h3><p>"I envision a totally transformed regional housing market that has enough 'transit-oriented' housing options to finally meet the overwhelming demand for families to be able to afford to live and work near a bus or rail station," says <b>Dan Lurie, president and CEO of Metropolitan Planning Council</b>.</p><p><b>Juan Sebastian, executive director of Elevated Chicago</b>, agrees.</p><p>"My dream investment for NITA is creating the nation’s leading equitable transit-oriented development program, helping communities build more affordable homes, local businesses and vibrant public spaces near transit."</p><h3>Bus corridors on Western, Ashland avenues</h3><p>"Chicago is primed and ready to benefit from bus rapid transit on Western Avenue," says <b>Amy Rynell, executive president of the Active Transportation Alliance</b>. "BRT creates a train-like transit experience for a fraction of the cost of heavy rail. Dedicated lanes, pre-paid boarding, train-like stations and smart traffic signals all combine to speed up the bus and provide a fast, reliable and affordable alternative to driving.<i>"</i></p><p>Add Ashland Avenue to the list of north-south roads primed for a dedicated bus corridor, says <b>Andrew Mack, an organizer</b> of the Bridgeport Kidical Mass Family Bike Ride and a founding member of the 11th Ward Safe Streets Union. "It has long been clear that a transportation system based on private cars is a poor plan for moving millions of people around our city. Bus rapid transit lines on Ashland and Western should be fast-tracked by NITA. The city that works needs to also be the city that moves."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Build downtown Metra tunnel, more frequent service</h3><p>NITA should connect downtown Metra lines through a series of tunnels, says <b>Peter Tucic, vice president of public policy for the Chicago Lighthouse</b>, which advocates for the blind. The idea for crosstown Metra service is called the STAR:Line and has been long promoted by <a class="Link" href="https://buildthetunnelchicago.org/" target="_blank" >a blog promoting #BuildTheTunnel</a>. "Now that NITA exists, we have an opportunity to create real alignment among the region’s three transit systems," Tucic says.</p><p><b>Rick Harnish, executive director of the High Speed Rail Alliance</b>, wants Metra service to be electrified and run more frequently so it's not just for commuters. "That would mean trains departing every 15 minutes or better. Metra Electric, especially the South Chicago Branch, is the best place for an early success."</p><h3>Connect Union Station and Blue Line</h3><p>"Fast-track a high-quality tunnel from Chicago Union Station to the Blue Line's Clinton Station, with prominent signage and, if space allows, a moving sidewalk," says <b>Joseph Schwieterman, director of DePaul University's Chaddick Institute for Metropolitan Development</b>. "This would be an important step toward more fully integrating Metra/Amtrak and CTA rail. The tunnel would also improve access to the Intercity Bus Station, which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/17/greyhound-bus-terminal-flixbus" target="_blank" >purchased by the city in August</a>."</p><h3>Community spaces near L stations</h3><p>NITA should build community spaces near the four proposed Red Line extension stations, says <b>Olatunji Oboi Reed, president and CEO of Equiticity</b>. This nonprofit calls them <a class="Link" href="https://www.equiticity.org/blog/-the-go-hub" target="_blank" >“Go Hubs”</a> — buildings that serve as community spaces where people can get access e-bikes and other ways to complete their trips to and from home. "Our goal is achieving racial equity, mobility justice, environmental justice and community ownership, translating physical mobility into upward social mobility," Reed says.</p><h3>Instead of a dream project, focus on fiscal responsibility</h3><p>"I am looking for NITA to be a good steward of taxpayers’ dollars," says<b> Ian Savage, professor of economics and transportation at Northwestern University</b>. "That means getting the operating agencies to get their existing infrastructure into a state of good repair and ensuring seamless transfers between a coordinated network of bus, L and regional rail services. I think NITA needs to demonstrate operational and fiscal responsibility on existing services before spending public money on expansionist proposals."</p><h3>What do you think?</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-e80000" name="html-embed-module-e80000"></a><div class="contribly-contribute-v2" data-client="b20193c8-5c0c-4a5b-a770-64305c544c4e" data-assignment="c248a6dc-070b-454b-84f6-5ebe9f47009e" data-display="inline" data-language="en-gb"></div><script type="text/javascript" src="https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/contribly-widgets/contribute/contribute-v2.5.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Demanda de la familia de Silverio Villegas González pide daños y perjuicios por su muerte por ICE
entries.summary: <p>La familia de Silverio Villegas González, el hombre que un agente de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) le disparó y lo mató durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, presentó el jueves una demanda administrativa en busca de una compensación del gobierno federal por su muerte.</p><p>José Villegas González, hermano de Villegas González, presentó la reclamación en virtud de la ley Federal Tort Claims Act en nombre del patrimonio de su hermano, solicitando una compensación por su “muerte injusta”. La reclamación es un paso obligatorio antes de demandar al gobierno federal.</p><p>Jonathan Manes, abogado del MacArthur Justice Center que representa a la familia, dijo que esperan pedir “una suma muy grande de dinero”, aunque no quiso revelar el monto total.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La reclamación incluye unos $10,000 por daños al automóvil de Villegas González y a sus pertenencias, aunque eso es aparte de la compensación por el sufrimiento que padeció y por las pérdidas emocionales y económicas de la familia.</p><p>“No estamos enfocados en la cifra en este momento”, dijo Manes. “Se trata de conocer la verdad y de exigir responsabilidades por lo que le pasó a Silverio”.</p><p>La demanda alega que dos agentes de ICE crearon una confrontación peligrosa y le dispararon a Villegas González cuando pudieron haberse apartado de su automóvil. También acusa a ICE y a funcionarios del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) de no haber capacitado ni supervisado adecuadamente a sus agentes.</p><p>Villegas González, de 38 años, había emigrado de México y vivió en Estados Unidos durante unos 18 años antes de morir. Trabajaba como cocinero y criaba a dos hijos.</p><p>Había dejado a sus hijos en la escuela y en la guardería y se dirigía al trabajo el 12 de septiembre de 2025, cuando los dos agentes de ICE intentaron detener su automóvil en Franklin Park y uno de ellos le disparó a Villegas González. Más tarde murió en el Loyola University Medical Center.</p><p>Después del tiroteo, DHS dijo que Villegas González había huido de una parada de tránsito y había arrastrado a un agente “una distancia considerable”. El departamento dijo que el agente resultó gravemente herido y abrió fuego porque temía por su vida.</p><p>Pero imágenes de la cámara corporal de la policía obtenidas por el Chicago Sun-Times mostraron al agente describiendo sus lesiones como “nada grave”. Su compañero informó una lesión en la rodilla y cortes en las manos.</p><p>La denuncia presentada por la familia de Villegas González se basa en video de vigilancia, grabaciones policiales e informes de ambulancia y de autopsia para cuestionar la versión del gobierno.</p><p>Manes dijo que el gobierno defendió el tiroteo antes de que pudiera investigar lo ocurrido.</p><p>“Ese mismo día en que mataron a Silverio, antes de que pudiera haber cualquier tipo de investigación, ya lo estaban calificando como justificado”, dijo.</p><p>Cuando Villegas González intentó alejarse conduciendo, el agente del lado del conductor de su automóvil se aferró a la ventana en lugar de apartarse, dijo Manes.</p><p>“No está en el camino del vehículo”, dijo Manes. “Y dispararle a Silverio no hace más que matarlo y dejar el carro completamente fuera de control”.</p><p>“La política de DHS confirma que no se le puede disparar a una persona solo porque se está alejando manejando”, añadió.</p><p>José Villegas González busca una compensación en nombre del patrimonio de su hermano por el dolor y sufrimiento antes de morir y por el “sufrimiento mental” de la familia, incluida la pérdida por parte de sus hijos del apoyo “emocional” y “económico” de su padre, según la denuncia.</p><p>Manes dijo que Villegas González tuvo dificultades para respirar y seguir con vida después de recibir un disparo en el cuello.</p><p>La compensación beneficiaría a los hijos y al cónyuge de Villegas González, no a su hermano, dijo Manes. La reclamación describe a Villegas González como el principal cuidador de sus hijos. Después de su muerte, los niños fueron colocados en un hogar de acogida en Idaho, lejos de sus familiares en el área de Chicago.</p><p>DHS dijo al Sun-Times en julio que los fiscales federales decidieron no presentar cargos contra el agente que le disparó y mató a Villegas González. Los funcionarios federales aún no han explicado públicamente por qué. Manes dijo que la familia no ha recibido un informe del incidente ni los nombres de los agentes involucrados.</p><p>La denuncia alega que el FBI tomó el control de la investigación poco después del tiroteo, pero no llevó a cabo una investigación adecuada.</p><p>En un comunicado, el FBI dijo que “respondió al incidente en Franklin Park y brindó asistencia a las autoridades en el lugar”, pero se negó a confirmar o negar si existe una investigación, citando la política del Departamento de Justicia (DOJ).</p><p>Franklin Park esperó más de siete meses para pedir a la Policía Estatal de Illinois que investigara, y lo hizo el mismo día en que la Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois publicó un informe demoledor sobre Midway Blitz.</p><p>La investigación estatal sigue abierta.</p><p>“Un año no ha borrado ni disminuido el dolor que sentimos por su ausencia”, dijeron José Villegas González y su esposa, Ana Villegas, en un comunicado en septiembre.</p><p>La demanda por daños y perjuicios le da a DHS y al FBI la oportunidad de revisar las acusaciones y considerar un acuerdo. Si el gobierno la rechaza o no toma una decisión final en un plazo de seis meses, la familia puede seguir adelante con una demanda.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Suspects in Englewood CTA bus shooting that left passengers, 57 and 65, injured due in court
entries.summary: <p>A man and a woman have been charged with a shooting aboard a CTA bus sparked over a seat last week that left bystanders 57 and 65 wounded late last month in Englewood.</p><p>Tyrese Jones, 19, and Destiny Jones, 18, were charged with attempted murder, aggravated battery and aggravated battery to a transit passenger, police said. <br>The two were scheduled for a detention hearing Friday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse. It was unclear if they are related. </p><p>Tyrese Jones, of Mundelein, and Destiny Jones is of the Grand Boulevard neighborhood. </p><p>They were identified as the people who, on Sept. 30, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/30/2-hospitalized-after-being-hit-by-gunfire-while-on-cta-bus" target="_blank" >allegedly participated in shooting </a>and seriously injuring a 57-year-old man and a 65-year-old woman, both of whom were passengers aboard the CTA bus in the 300 block of West 63rd Street, police said. </p><p>An <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/aspiring-paramedic-recalls-how-a-cta-bus-seat-dispute-turned-into-shooting" target="_blank" >aspiring paramedic who witnessed the attack</a> told the Sun-Times he was on his way home from work when a man and woman began fighting with another passenger over a wet seat, according to the witness and police reports obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>“Basically, the lady wanted him to get up, and he didn’t want to get up, so she apparently got to swinging on him,” the witness said.</p><p>When the argument turned physical, the seated passenger reportedly pulled a gun and fired, authorities said.</p>

entries.title: Feds appear to hide name of government lawyer in new 'Broadview Six' court filings
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago appeared<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>to be hiding the name of an attorney representing<b> </b>the United States government<b> </b>in the ongoing legal fight over the doomed "Broadview Six" case, originally brought against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros' office filed<b> </b>two<b> </b>partially redacted documents overnight<b>, </b>seeking U.S. District Judge April<b> </b>Perry's permission<b> </b>to disclose grand jury transcripts<b> </b>and<b> </b>exhibits. It cited the Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure requiring grand jury secrecy<b> </b>as one reason to hide portions of the documents from the public.</p><p>The documents were filed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas<b> </b>Walsh, the head of Boutros' civil division. But the feds made the unusual move of covering up what appeared to be the signature block of a second attorney representing the U.S. government.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" >‘Broadview Six’ judge wants to put prosecutors under oath, keeps contempt charges on the table</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Representatives of Boutros' office and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday morning. Grand jury transcripts in the case have already been made public, something Perry noted on the court docket after Boutros' request was apparently first made under seal earlier this week. </p><p>It is highly unusual for the name of a government attorney to be redacted from such a document. Even in the Chicago prosecution of violent Sinaloa cartel figures, the names of Justice Department attorneys appear on the public record, along with their professional contact information.</p><p>It's particularly striking in the "Broadview Six" case, in which Boutros' office has already been accused of a cover-up. </p><p>Perry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >announced last week</a> that<b> </b>further<b> </b>“under oath”<b> </b>fact-finding is necessary in the tainted case. In doing so, she left open the possibility of naming a special prosecutor<b> </b>to investigate Boutros and other Justice Department officials.</p><p>That means the threat of a criminal investigation continues to hang over what was once seen as a top-tier U.S. attorney’s office, where the mantra has long been “do the right thing.”</p><p>Perry announced her intention at the end of an hourlong hearing<b> </b>in which she asked an attorney for Boutros’ office whether any of the prosecutors who worked on the politically charged “Broadview Six” case would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.</p><p>He didn’t rule it out.</p><p>Perry told the lawyers, “My sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.” The comment was likely designed to avoid separation-of-powers concerns from derailing her inquiry.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Charged were then-congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b> </b>campaign<b> </b>worker<b> </b>Andre Martin.</p><p>The case against them collapsed on May 21, after Perry alleged that Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg spoke to grand jurors outside the grand jury room and put her personal credibility on the line to support charges. The judge also indicated Mecklenburg had excused grand jurors who disagreed with the feds’ case, a claim Mecklenburg denies.</p><p>Mecklenburg recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/24/broadview-six-sheri-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >retired from the Justice Department</a> in order to defend herself, insisting that she followed the instructions of Boutros’ front office<b> </b>“at every turn.”</p><p>But Perry said she found “most problematic” the fact that the apparent misconduct was redacted out of transcripts initially given to her by Boutros’ office. The redactions were made after Mecklenburg withdrew from the case.</p>

entries.title: Cubs’ Matt Shaw among featured speakers at conservative political event later this year
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> utility man Matt Shaw is listed among the featured speakers at a conservative political event in December.</p><p>The event, hosted by Turning Point USA – the group founded by controversial podcaster and influencer Charlie Kirk, who was shot and killed last year – features many other political and media figures associated with President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement, including Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The first speaker drop of AmericaFest 2026 is HERE 🔥<br><br>Restore the culture. Reclaim America.<br><br>Be there: <a href="https://t.co/kMi2p7BBuS">https://t.co/kMi2p7BBuS</a> <a href="https://t.co/L5OJtsGL4S">pic.twitter.com/L5OJtsGL4S</a></p>— Turning Point USA (@TPUSA) <a href="https://x.com/TPUSA/status/2108256133593104463?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Shaw, who notably <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/21/cubs-third-baseman-matt-shaw-leaves-team-to-attend-charlie-kirk-memorial-service" >left the Cubs to attend Kirk’s memorial service</a> last September, became friends with Kirk, an Arlington Heights native, while the two lived in the same apartment complex in Arizona.</p><p>“The reason Charlie and I connected so close was because of our faith,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/23/cubs-matt-shaw-charlie-kirk-memorial-leaving-team-meant-to-be" >Shaw said after returning to the team</a> last season. “That’s something that drives me every single day, something that I think about all the time.</p><p>“So if people are wondering who I am and what I stand for, I’d say that my faith and the many blessings I’ve been given is why I’m able to be here. And I just want to make sure that I can give that back to people, that I can support people around me, that I can love people around me the same way that I’ve been blessed.”</p><p>Shaw was the Cubs’ everyday third baseman during the 2025 season, but he was relegated to a bench role after the team signed two-time World Series champion Alex Bregman to a free-agent contract last offseason.</p><p>Some of Shaw’s offensive numbers improved this season, though that came in limited time, with multiple injuries keeping him to just 77 games.</p><p>Whether Shaw, who appeared in 34 games in the outfield during the 2026 season, factors more heavily into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/03/four-offseason-questions-facing-jed-hoyer-cubs-who-have-pitching-at-top-of-lengthy-to-do-list" >the Cubs’ plans for 2027</a> remains to be seen. The team could be searching to fill two holes in the outfield, with left fielder Ian Happ and right fielder Seiya Suzuki slated to hit free agency.</p><p>Team president Jed Hoyer said last week that both Shaw and fellow reserve infielder Pedro Ramirez could play larger roles in the future.</p><p>“Having Pedro and Matt, super versatile, both really good players, we can ask more of them going forward,” Hoyer said. “We didn’t have to this year, given the nature of our corner outfield. But I think they both can certainly do that, and we’ll lean on both those guys more heavily going forward.”</p>

old-school horror.</p><p>Among the offerings: Otherworld Theatre's world premiere of "Midsummer Night Scream" is a new take on Shakespeare's most-produced play, giving it a 1980s, neon-and-synth-filled rework.</p><p>Relatedly, the Broadway in Chicago remount of Kokandy’s hit musical "Jekyll & Hyde" is a gothic horror story fueled by a 15-piece orchestra backing 1980s power ballads. The set feels like a haunted house.</p><p>Take a gander, if you dare, at our list of nine must-see shows this spooky season.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtthjhk-l-ii/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><h4></h4><p><b>What's a Chicago ghost story or urban legend that you grew up hearing about?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). Daley of Chicago' by Mike Royko, the best Chicago columnist ever. This is a fact-based review of Daley from cradle to grave — outstanding! An explanation of the city during Daley's reign also, published in '71. A must-read for every Chicagoan." — <i>Michael King</i></p><p>"'The Chicago Way' by Michael Harvey, author of the Michael Kelly series, is a gripping story. It's filled with familiar landmarks and institutions." — <i>Jay Massey</i></p><p>"The Studs Lonigan trilogy; ('Young Lonigan,' 'The Young Manhood of Studs Lonigan' and 'Judgement Day') by James T. Farrell, for many a forgotten but brilliant Chicago writer who provided readers with an honest portrait of the personal and professional lives of Chicago citizenry in the early 20th century." — <i><u>Tom Knoff</u></i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu<br><b>Copy edited by</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' season could follow one of two paths: 2025-26 Sharks or 2021-22 Hawks
entries.summary: <p>The Blackhawks begin a seven-game home stand Saturday that could determine the trajectory of their season.</p><p>At 1-4-0, it hasn't started with much success, but their play has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/08/blackhawks-islanders-improved-performance-nhl" >improved</a> substantially in the last two games. Time will tell if that's a blip or the beginning of a broader trend.</p><p>If it's the latter, this 2026-27 Hawks season could follow a trajectory similar to the 2025-26 Sharks' season. If it's the former, this Hawks season could instead play out more like the 2021-22 Hawks.</p><p>It could also easily end up in the middle, but considering October is prime overreaction time around the NHL, it's worth examining the two extreme possibilities.</p><h3><b>2025-26 Sharks’ trajectory</b></h3><p>Last season marked the fourth consecutive season that the Sharks began with a losing streak of five games or longer — a remarkable stat. When they were 0-4-2 after six games last October, nobody batted an eye.</p><p>They had conceded 29 goals over the six games, and their analytics were no better. They had a 37.0% expected-goals ratio and 40.4% scoring-chance ratio during five-on-five play.</p><p>Then a wild 6-5 overtime win over the Rangers in the Sharks' seventh game jumpstarted an 8-2-1 hot streak that did raise eyebrows around the league — and, looking back, marked the moment the Sharks' rebuild turned a corner.</p><p>They ultimately flirted with the playoffs deep into March, wooed fans with an exciting playing style, established Macklin Celebrini as a superstar and finished 39-35-8, equating to a whopping 34-point improvement from 2024-25.</p><p>The Hawks and Sharks have been compared ad nauseam in recent years, and even though the Sharks' surge last season pushed them ahead in that debate, the Hawks could theoretically catch up this season. They have the youth, talent and potential to do so if things start clicking.</p><p>And what would be a more logical time for things to start clicking than a long home stand after settling into the season? </p><p>The Hawks' lineup has found some chemistry, former top-three picks Artyom Levshunov and Anton Frondell seem to be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/08/blackhawks-artyom-levshunov-following-instincts-blues-anton-frondell" >developing</a> steadily and it's possible Connor Bedard could return by the end of the month.</p><p>Four of the opponents coming to Chicago — the Hurricanes, Stars, Canadiens and Panthers — are tough, but the the Sharks beat the Wild twice and Avalanche once during their hot streak last fall. That's simply what it takes to ascend the hierarchy.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Joe Hrycych/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>2021-22 Hawks’ trajectory</b></h3><p>Most Hawks fans will be familiar with this comparison, and it won't bring back pleasant memories.</p><p>The Hawks entered 2021-22 with a radically reshuffled lineup (headlined by Seth Jones and Marc-Andre Fleury) and immediately embarrassed themselves.</p><p>They lost their first consecutive nine games, and they were 1-9-2 on Nov. 6 when then-interim general manager Kyle Davidson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2021/11/6/22767160/blackhawks-fire-jeremy-colliton-coaching-change-derek-king-kyle-davidson" >fired</a> then-coach Jeremy Colliton. </p><p>Granted, dark clouds hung over this 2021-22 Hawks team that aren't relevant to the 2026-27 Hawks. Ex-GM Stan Bowman had resigned on Oct. 26 during the fallout from the sexual-assault scandal, and Colliton had run an exhausting training camp that predictably backfired.</p><p>But the team's analytics when Colliton got axed — 41.0% expected-goals ratio and 43.3% scoring-chance ratio — were actually slightly better than the current Hawks' ratios: 37.8% and 40.8%, respectively.</p><p>Interim coach Derek King took over and mildly improved the vibes for the rest of a hopeless, purposeless season, which the Hawks finished 28-42-12.</p><p>For now, Davidson and current Hawks coach Jeff Blashill possess much stronger job security than Bowman and Colliton did. With portions of the fan base already expressing frustration, however, that could change if 2026-27 plays out even half as disastrously as 2021-22 did.</p><p>The coming weeks should make it clearer in which direction this season will go, for better or worse.</p>

entries.summary: <p>It doesn't matter how many years it's been since the 1985 Super Bowl championship or the run of Bill Swersky's Superfans on "Saturday Night Live" — former Bears head coach Mike Ditka is and always has been an icon. entries.title: Bears RB Kyle Monangai ruled out for Packers game
entries.summary: <p>The NFL's best rushing offense will look different Sunday.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back Kyle Monangai, who ran a whopping 30 times for 146 yards against the Jets, will miss Sunday's game at Lambeau Field, coach Ben Johnson said. He has turf toe, for which he has seen a specialist. He's in a walking boot. The Bears don't plan to put him on injured reserve, which would keep him out four games, but, rather, consider him "week-to-week." </p><p>Earlier this week, Johnson said he'd be careful with Monangai's practice workload given how sore he was after the team played 89 snaps. That soreness was, in fact, an injury.</p><p>Johnson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/08/bears-report-rb-dandre-swift-kyle-monangai-out-practice-injury-toe-thumb-nfl" target="_blank" >benched D’Andre Swift </a>because he fumbled in the third quarter against the Jets. That punishment doesn't figure to continue. He'll start with Roschon Johnson likely serving as the change-of-pace back.</p><p>Swift was held out of Wednesday's practice with a knee/hip injury but returned Thursday. He said he understood the benching and said fumbling "ain't me." </p><p>Johnson seemed ready to move on from the mistake, too.</p><p>"I'm not concerned about anything other than him getting his body back underneath him and ready to go," Johnson said of Swift. "And I think [Thursday] he proved that he's going to be able to help us here this weekend. So I'm very optimistic about that."<br></p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson: Mike Ditka was 'gold standard'
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' navy-and-orange flag, festooned with a football for every championship the team has won, flew at half staff Friday at Halas Hall.</p><p>Inside the Bears practice facility, their current head coach praised their iconic one just hours after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" target="_blank" >Mike Ditka</a> died at age 86.</p><p>"As far as I’m concerned. Coach Ditka is the gold standard in terms of this place," Johnson said Friday. "He’s a legend around here as a player, as a coach. His impact is still being felt to this day. As the head coach of the Bears I feel humbled to be in that same chair he was once in. It’s a sad day."</p><p>Johnson never met Ditka but saw his image plastered all over Halas Hall, including the player's entrance.</p><p>"I don’t know if there’s been a head coach with that much — other than, obviously, George Halas — but that much success just for, I think it was 11 years and the number of winning seasons, the win/loss record, obviously a Super Bowl winner," he said. "As a head coach, it’s been hard to replicate that since his time, certainly as a player as well."</p><p>Johnson had yet to address the team about Ditka's passing but said he would at some point before Sunday's game against the rival Packers at Lambeau Field.</p><p>"I mean, that defense there in the ’80s, I mean, that was something to behold," Johnson said. "And, you know, we keep talking about the 'Monsters of the Midway' and how much we'd like to bring that back. And they were the standard, and they have been for some time. But I think he had a lot to do with that, that mindset. Certainly, they were great players, but that head coach was, he was special, a special individual."</p><p>In a statement, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said Ditka "brought intensity, authenticity, and an unmistakable personality to everything he did." He praised his work with the Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund, which helped former players, and called him an "ambassador for the game" who "inspired generations of fans."<br></p>

entries.title: 'Da Coach' Mike Ditka embodied Chicago, the city he adopted
entries.summary: <p>Iron Mike. Oh, man.</p><p>A part of every football fan just died with “Da Coach” himself.</p><p>Myself, I can’t believe he’s gone. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" >Mike Ditka died Friday at 86.</a></p><p>Somehow the guy seemed immortal, like an Easter Island statue, like a high rift in the granite mantle of the Earth itself.</p><p>Every Chicagoan is diminished in some way with Mike Ditka not here anymore.</p><p>Was the guy perfect? Ha! Not even close.</p><p>But, brother, was he a competitor, a character, a warm, caring, nasty, walking, talking whirlwind of ferocity, tenderness and crazy contradictions. Kind of like this city itself, the Chicago he adopted despite his roots in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania.</p><p>I mean, Ditka didn’t just wear his heart on his sleeve; the dude wore it on a banner he carried high above him, daring anyone to say he was wrong about anything, to challenge him, to show they had more passion for his beloved game of football and winning and stomping the earth than he did.</p><p>A decade ago, I asked him about life moving so fast — days long, maybe, but years flying by. He grinned that slight, somewhat impish grin he had, behind that mustache he kept even when mustaches weren’t cool, the bristle brush that became part of his logo, in that face of his that truly resembled a bear’s. He’d thought about the ending.</p><p>“I’m coming around third in this life,” he said, “going for home with a headfirst slide.”</p><p>Is that not perfect?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>Everything Ditka did — be it playing football, coaching, selling products, yakking on TV, golfing, dealing cards for gin rummy, pontificating on anything under the sun — he did headfirst. That’s the only way he knew to move forward.</p><p>Don’t forget he was a very good baseball player, too — and if he’d been as passionate about hitting a ball as he was about hitting safeties, it’s possible he could have gone far in that sport. Ponder this: you’re a catcher and a full-tilt Ditka, sans helmet, is coming at you from third base, headfirst, flat-topped noggin looking like a blacksmith’s anvil.</p><p>Help!</p><p>I mean, here’s where we stop and laugh the good laugh. Which is what Ditka would want us all to do.</p><p>Because he had a sense of humor. And he was self-deprecating and able to make fun of his flaws and juvenile rages and petty grievances. When he broke his right hand after punching a locker after a tough Bears loss and then the next week told his players pregame, “Win one for Lefty,” that’s good stuff.</p><p>It’s why Chicago loved him. We love winners. We love guys who lay it all on the line. But we don’t like phonies or stuck-up snobs or cocky rich athletes who don’t appreciate hard work and the meaning of giving your all.</p><p>Sometimes Ditka went from one side of the fence to the other, and maybe even back again, depending on his mood. His dad was a steel mill union laborer in Aliquippa, but Mike continued to coach the Bears even when scab players crossed the picket line in 1987. Then he defended the union and all retired players when the head trauma issues came to the fore and too many ex-players faced physical and financial ruin.</p><p>He blamed himself often for his impetuousness. After he retaliated against the Lions in 1985 for a perceived slight in an earlier game by having Dave Duerson take out Detroit kicker Eddie Murray on a legal but unneeded hit, he felt guilty. “I was younger and madder than they were,” he told me years later of the Lions coaches.</p><p>But anger isn’t his lasting legacy.</p><p>Genuineness is. And passion. And winning. (That Super XX championship team recedes like a vapor, doesn’t it?)</p><p>But above all, Ditka, oddly, reminds us of love. He had so much of it sometimes, for so many things, he nearly exploded.</p><p>What a lovely man he was.</p>

entries.title: Mike Ditka, who coached the Bears to their only Super Bowl championship, has died
entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka, the Hall of Fame tight end who played on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> 1963 NFL championship team and coached the team to its only Super Bowl championship after the 1985 season, has died. He was 86.</p><p>He died about 9 a.m. Friday surrounded by family and friends, a family spokesperson said.</p><p>A statement issued by the family said that "while the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever."</p><p>As a player, a coach and a larger-than-life personality who invigorated a generation of Bears fans, Ditka left an indelible mark on the Chicago sporting landscape — from the playing field to sports talk to pop culture — that few can match. Of Chicago’s impressive list of Hall of Fame athletes — Sid Luckman, Walter Payton, Bobby Hull, Ernie Banks, Stan Mikita, Frank Thomas among the all-time greats — only Michael Jordan can challenge Ditka’s legacy as a local sports icon.</p><p>As a Bears legend, Ditka was one of the last direct links to George Halas, the Bears’ founder and owner. Halas drafted Ditka out of Pittsburgh in 1961. And even after a falling out that led to Halas trading Ditka in the prime of Ditka’s career in 1967, Halas hand-picked Ditka to coach the Bears in 1982. Four years later, Halas was gone (he died in 1983), but Ditka led the Bears to victory in Super Bowl XX in the midst of the best run of Bears success since winning four NFL titles from 1940-47 with Luckman at quarterback.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>Nearly 40 years after that glorious 1985 season, the team hasn’t had even a semblance of the Ditka-era success. In 31 seasons since Ditka was fired by team president Michael McCaskey in 1993, the Bears have yet to have even three consecutive playoff seasons or three consecutive winning seasons.</p><p>The son of an ex-Marine, Michael Keller Ditka grew up in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, 20 miles northwest of Pittsburgh, and was a three-sport star — football, basketball and baseball — at Aliquippa High School. As a shortstop, he attracted interest from the Cincinnati Reds and Milwaukee Braves as a senior. But he opted for football and chose Pitt over Notre Dame and Penn State.</p><h3>Impact player</h3><p>Ditka also played basketball and baseball at Pitt, but it was clear that football was his future. As a senior, Ditka was a first-team All-American at end. He was the defensive star in Pitt’s 10-0 upset of No. 3 Syracuse, ending the defending national champion Orangemen’s 16-game winning streak. His 59-yard catch paved the way for a victory over No. 14 Notre Dame the following week. And the week after that, Ditka blocked a punt in a 7-7 tie with No. 12 Army.</p><p>“He is the best college player in the country,” Pittsburgh Steelers coach Buddy Parker said of Ditka.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/0T-Q7fFCAgo?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Pitt Athletics | HOF 2018 | Mike Ditka"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Parker likely wanted Ditka for the hometown Steelers and nearly had the chance. The Bears selected Ditka with the fifth overall pick of the 1961 draft (conducted Dec. 27, 1960) — after winning a coin flip with the Steelers.</p><p>Halas was looking to capitalize on Ditka’s outstanding blocking ability, but quickly realized he had much more than that in the 6-3, 230-pound end. Combining his size, strength, athleticism with his own brand of relentless aggressiveness, Ditka transformed the end position into a pass-catching, big-play role rarely seen before in the NFL.</p><p>He had 56 receptions for 1,076 yards (19.2 yards per catch) and a franchise-record-tying 12 touchdowns as a rookie in 1961 — winning the NFL Rookie of the Year Award.</p><p>Ditka made the Pro Bowl his first five seasons with the Bears and was named first-team All-Pro in 1963 and 1964. His 75 receptions (for 897 yards and five touchdowns) in 1964 set an NFL record for a tight end that lasted for 16 seasons, until the Chargers’ Kellen Winslow had 89 receptions in 1980.</p><p>But Ditka became disenchanted in 1966, when he had just 32 receptions for 378 yards and two touchdowns and, claiming a “clash of personalities” with Halas, signed a three-year contract with the AFL’s Houston Oilers. Before the Bears could challenge the legality of that move — the AFL and NFL were in the process of a merger — Halas traded Ditka to the Eagles for quarterback Jack Concannon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7XmIW0rp-1w?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="WFAA Interview with the Dallas Cowboys' Mike Ditka"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Ditka played two seasons with the Eagles and four with the Cowboys, but never had the same impact. He did win a Super Bowl with the Cowboys, catching a seven-yard touchdown pass to complete a 24-3 victory over the Dolphins in Super Bowl VI in Dallas’ 24-3 victory after the 1971 season.</p><h3>Move to the sideline</h3><h3></h3><p>Ditka retired after the 1972 season — his 427 career receptions were the most by an NFL tight end at the time. He immediately became a special teams and wide receivers coach for the Cowboys and coach Tom Landry. He was never considered a major candidate for a head coaching job, but always had his eye on the Bears.</p><p>“In 1978, I wrote Mr. Halas a letter,” Ditka said in his book, “In Life, First You Kick Ass,” written with Sun-Times columnist Rick Telander. “I was the special teams coach for the Cowboys and I was no big deal. Maybe I was a little wild. But what I said in the letter was, ‘We didn’t part on the best of terms when you traded me, but I would love to come back some day, back to Chicago. And be the head coach. I’m not ready yet, but I will be some day. I’ll bring back Chicago Bears tradition and pride. I promise.’”</p><p>Halas took Ditka’s sentiment to heart. In 1982, after consecutive seasons of 7-9 and 6-10, he fired coach Neill Armstrong and hired Ditka.</p><p>“I believe everyone has a destiny in life and mine is with the Chicago Bears,” Ditka said at the press conference announcing his hiring.</p><p>The timing was just right. With general manager Jim Finks building the roster with young talent (Dan Hampton, Otis Wilson, Matt Suhey, Mike Singletary, Keith Van Horne to go with star Walter Payton), the Bears added Jim McMahon in 1982 and a stellar 1983 draft class that included future Hall of Famers Richard Dent and Jimbo Covert.</p><p>They were ready for takeoff. The Bears went 10-6 and reached the NFC Championship game in 1984, then went 15-1 and won the Super Bowl in 1985 — one of the best NFL teams of all time. That was the start of an eight-season run in which the Bears went 90-37 and made the playoffs seven times.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Bears head coach Mike Ditka is carried off the field by Steve McMichael, left, and William Perry after the Bears win Super Bowl XX in New Orleans on Jan. 26, 1986.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Phil Sandlin/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>They never got back to the Super Bowl, though. And on a team of personalities and egos, Ditka’s own personality and ego played a part in the demise of that era. After going 5-11 in 1992, Ditka was fired by team president Michael McCaskey.</p><p>As it turned out, Ditka and the Bears were never better than when they were together. Ditka was hired to coach the Saints in 1997, but went 6-10, 6-10 and 3-13 and was fired after three seasons.</p><h3>Pop star</h3><p>Ditka’s popularity never waned. In fact, it continued to grow as the Bears futilely struggled to recapture the glory of the Ditka era. Ditka stayed in the public eye by doing NFL analysis on ESPN, CBS and NBC and radio stations, including WMVP-AM in Chicago.</p><p>The Ditka legend continued to be self-perpetuating. The “Superfans” skit on Saturday Night Live in the 1990s that was inspired by Bears fans’ almost irrational reverence for Ditka has itself sustained the fans’ love for “Da Coach.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/B9NO24hbe8Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Bill Swerski’s Superfans: Bears vs. Giants - SNL"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Ditka was noticeably absent at major Bears events in recent years because of declining health. He did not attend Steve McMichael's induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in August 2024 and was not one of the myriad members of the 1985 Bears honored in person at Soldier Field during the 40th anniversary season.</p><p>During the lead up to the Super Bowl in February, McMahon said Ditka would have been the perfect teammate because he played the game the right way.</p><p></p><p>"Had he been in my huddle, he would’ve understood me a hell of a lot better," he told the Sun-Times. "He would’ve known I actually do know what I’m doing and we wouldn’t have fought so much. We probably would’ve hung out more than anybody.</p><p></p><p>"He’s going to be missed. He made his mark in this world and in this league being who he was.”</p><p>That’s the kind of effect that made Ditka more than just another popular player or coach. There might someday be another personality who matches his accomplishments. But there will never be another Mike Ditka. He’ll be remembered for his best moments and his worst, and for his indomitable spirit that was both a strength and a flaw. But he never will be forgotten.</p><p><i>Steve Greenberg contributed.</i></p>

entries.title: Arrest made in CTA janitor’s fatal stabbing at Damen Green Line station
entries.summary: <p>A person of interest has been taken into police custody after a CTA janitor was fatally stabbed during an argument at a CTA train station on the Near West Side Thursday afternoon, police said.</p><p>Charges have not been announced. </p><p>Julian Mobley, 41, was at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/08/05/cta-damen-green-line-station" target="_blank" >Damen Green Line CTA station</a> in the 2000 block of West Lake Street around 3 p.m. when another man approached and began an argument, according to Chicago police and ATU Local 308, the union that represents CTA workers, including Mobley. </p><p>The men began fighting and the suspect stabbed Mobley in his neck with a sharp object, police said. He was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.</p><p>The suspect fled west, police said.</p><p>In a statement, the CTA said it was working to share video footage of the attack with investigators and extended condolences to the family of a beloved employee. </p><p>Service was restored on the Green Line around 8 p.m. Thursday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div afternoon</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"We extend our heartfelt condolences to our colleague’s family, loved ones and co-workers," the transit agency said. "We will support law enforcement officials’ efforts to ensure that the offender is apprehended and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law."</p><p>Mobley has been a member of Local 308 since 2018, according to union president Pennie McCoach. He was a father of two, a 14-year-old and an 18-month-old, and had been married to his wife for 20 years, she said.</p><p>Mobley was mild-mannered and kind, and his eyes lit up when he talked about his children, according to rail janitor and union board member Audrey Veasley.</p><p>"His character is, he was a gentleman," Veasley said during a news conference hours after the incident. "He was a real man."</p><p>McCoach said Mobley's death is another example of why more safety measures are needed for CTA workers and called for immediate action — such as a review of safety protocols, increased security and better training — from the transit authority. Mobley is the second CTA employee to be killed while on the job in the last several months. In June, CTA switchman Kevin Barlow was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/29/god-has-taken-his-angel-friends-and-family-mourn-cta-worker-fatally-shot-in-roseland" >shot and killed while on duty</a>.</p><p>"Let me be clear: This is not a tragedy, this is a safety failure," McCoach said. "Our members show up every single day to serve the people of Chicago. They keep this city moving. They deserve to return home safely. That is a basic right, not a privilege."</p><p>Crime on the CTA had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/08/cta-transit-crime-security-surge" >reportedly dropped for six consecutive months</a> earlier this year following beefed-up security due to a high number of violent crimes. But McCoach questioned the numbers released by the transit authority.</p><p>"I don't truly believe in what they're giving us because every day my phone rings some type of way that one of our members has been assaulted or harmed, and these types of incidents occur," she said. "The numbers, I don't think they're valid. I think they're fictitious and they're not real."</p>

entries.title: Bears fans mourn Mike Ditka, the man who unified city sports fans and 'taught Chicago to hate Green Bay'
entries.summary: <p>To Christopher Bartolini, Mike Ditka was the man who gathered his South Side neighborhood around his dad’s television in his family’s tiny living room — which had an antenna that still caught the Bears broadcast from Indiana stations when Chicago blacked out the games — every Sunday.</p><p>The morning <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" >Ditka’s death was announced</a>, Bartolini said he was thinking back to when Bears legend Dan Hampton stopped in at his restaurant a few weeks earlier and spoke highly of Ditka’s coaching.</p><p>“[Ditka] was always very passionate, and I think it’s something more people could bring to their lives,” Bartolini said. “The way he commanded that team and was so fiery, his attitude, he didn’t back down to anything.”</p><p>Fans around the city mourned the loss of "Da Coach" Friday, just days before the Chicago Bears are set to take on the Green Bay Packers, an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/09/bears-mike-ditka-die-packers-praise-fiercest-competitors-nfl-history" >intense rivalry Ditka helped solidify</a> as a player from 1961-1966 and then coach for a decade starting in 1982. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel hatred of the Packers, that 50-year Bears fan Rob Raczyk will remember Ditka by. He said the NFL Hall of Famer, who coached the team to its only Super Bowl championship in 1985, “was the first guy who taught Chicago fans to hate Green Bay.”</p><p>Amid a contentious month of October playoff baseball, Raczyk credited Ditka with uniting the Chicago sports community under one banner not only with the team’s historic Super Bowl win, but the way he flamed the rivalry with Green Bay in one simple phrase: “F--- the Packers.”</p><p>“Chicago hadn’t won before,” Raczyk said. “This was pre-Jordan and 2016 Cubs. He was bigger than life in a lot of regards. He transcended sports in Chicago. It doesn’t matter, you’re at Wrigley Field or Sox Park, and everyone chants it. Cubs and Sox fans don’t get along, but everyone hates the Packers. It’s our unifying factor.”</p><p>Los Angeles residents Andy Estrada and Johnny Montes, wearing Packers and Bears gear respectively, just happened to be driving by Soldier Field as they heard the news Friday morning from Estrada’s wife.</p><p>The father and son-in-law were in town as they prepared to go to the rival game Sunday in Green Bay, their first together after 15 years of planning to do so.</p><p>“Even though I’m a Packers fan, he’s legendary,” Estrada said. “Packers versus Bears is sort of like a holiday to us. The game’s gonna be a bit different Sunday. I think we’re all gonna be Packers fans.”</p><p> Montes' office wall is graced by an autographed poster of the team lifting Ditka above their heads, his own holy grail. He said it’ll be different to see the poster once he’s home in California, especially reflecting on the win depicted in the photo, which he witnessed live at 11 years old.</p><p>“When you think of the entries.title: Illinois' Bret Bielema needs a 'W.' Michigan State's Pat Fitzgerald does, too. Illini or Spartans?
entries.summary: <p>In Year 6 at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Illinois</a>, coach Bret Bielema — winner of 19 games over the last two seasons — didn’t have a dud of a 2026 campaign drawn up on the whiteboard.</p><p>There’s danger of just that, though, with the Illini at 2-3 after a sorry Homecoming loss to Big Ten doormat Purdue.</p><p>“Instead of being where we could be or should be or, in my mind, in a better place than where we’re at, we’re at 2-3,” Bielema said this week. “The thing we can’t do is let that make us fall to a lower place.”</p><p>In Year 1 at Michigan State, coach Pat Fitzgerald — whose last two Northwestern teams were 4-20 in 2021 and 2022 — has a stopgap roster most everyone figured would struggle. That hasn’t stopped Fitzgerald from getting aggravated as his Spartans also sit at 2-3.</p><p>“We’ve got to coach better, but they’ve got to frickin’ play better, too,” he said of his squad. “If we want to win, we’ve got to play better.”</p><p><b>Illinois (-2½) at Michigan State </b>(2:30 p.m., FS1, 890-AM) is a game each team probably has to win if it’s going to make something — anything — of itself this season. If the Illini can’t beat the Spartans, it’ll be a repudiation of everything Bielema has built downstate. If the Spartans can’t beat the Illini, it’ll remind a bunch of people that Fitzgerald hasn’t coached a winning team in quite a while.</p><p>It’s bad vs. bad or, at best, halfway decent vs. halfway decent. Still, I’m calling it a must-win week — for both.</p><p>Bielema has a leaky defense and a balky offense to worry about, though his combo of quarterback Katin Houser and wide receiver Collin Dixon already has hooked up for an impressive eight touchdowns. That pair could — should — go off in this matchup and is a big reason I lean toward the Illini.</p><p>The Spartans have the bottom-ranked offense among all Big Ten teams, making this a golden chance for Illini defenders to run out there at Spartan Stadium and act like they’ve played football before. (They have, haven’t they?)</p><p>Year 6 vs. Year 1 is supposed to be a mismatch when the latter team has started from scratch. By the fourth quarter, it will be. Make that might be. No, will be. I-L-L, 27-17.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The Pat Fitzgerald era at <a href="https://x.com/MSU_Football?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@MSU_Football</a> begins tonight 🗡️ <a href="https://t.co/269E24LbOT">pic.twitter.com/269E24LbOT</a></p>— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) <a href="https://x.com/CFBONFOX/status/2096026555898073143?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>OTHER WEEK 6 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>Ball State (+35½) at Northwestern </b>(11:30 a.m., BTN, 720-AM): Which Cardinals team will show up, the one that lost 56-3 at Ohio State in Week 1 or the one that has continued to get its facemask shoved in since then? Wait, those are the same teams. Wildcats, 45-7.</p><p><b>No. 1 Texas (-7½) vs. Oklahoma </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): You haven’t lived until you’ve taken in the Red River Rivalry at a half-burnt-orange, half-crimson Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas. The games have been famously unpredictable, though OU coach Brent Venables has gotten his butt roast handed to him in blowout fashion three times in four years since taking over. ’Horns, 24-13.</p><p><b>Stanford (+39½) at No. 3 Notre Dame </b>(2:30 p.m., NBC 5, 780-AM): Have I mentioned Stanford lost 57-3 at Wake Forest last time out? Seems relevant. Irish by merely 38.</p><p><b>No. 21 UCLA (+11½) at No. 13 Oregon </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): The unbeaten Bruins might be the most improved team in the Big Ten. Coach Bob Chesney didn’t just fall off the Curt Cignetti tree; he’s legit crushing it right now. But beating the Ducks in their home pond? That would be completely next-level. Ducks, 38-31.</p><p><b>No. 2 Georgia (+1½) at No. 6 Alabama </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): The Big Ten has been the biggest bopper the last few years, but the SEC might be better this time and, either way, this clash is hotter than two bobcats in a burlap sack. Georgia’s on my mind, 31-27.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 7 Indiana (-7) at Nebraska </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): I’d tell you how long it has been since Nebraska beat a ranked opponent, but you wouldn’t believe me. What does that leave for us to talk about? Fine — 0-for-31 over 10-plus years. Hoosiers make it 0-for-32.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>No. 19 USC (+1½) at Penn State </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5): Matt Campbell’s Nittany Lions “lack identity across the board,” the first-year coach said so himself this week. Trojans prove him right.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>5-1 straight-up, 5-1 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>27-9 straight-up, 18-18 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/08/chicago-white-sox-fans-blackout-cleveland-guardians-mlb-postseason-south-side-rate-field" target="_blank" >White Sox fans, does it get any better than this? Ben Johnson over Matt LaFleur, right? Is it Sunday yet? What could go wrong?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
