entries.title: White Sox right-hander Sean Burke tabbed to start do-or-die ALDS Game 5
entries.summary: <p>When working behind an opener for Game 2 of the American League Division Series, White Sox right-hander <b>Sean Burke</b> said “I dream of the World Series more than I dream of a playoff start.”</p><p>But as the Sox return to Cleveland for a win-or-go-home Game 5, Burke is getting that playoff start; one with the biggest stakes for the franchise in the last 20 years.</p><p>“I love being able to pitch in the big game,” Burke said on Friday. “That the coaching staff and the team trust me to go out there and do my thing [Saturday] just means the world to me.”</p><p>Peppering the zone with a riding mid-90s four-seam fastball that sizzled above the barrels of Guardians hitters, Burke threw 5 ⅓ innings of one-run ball in the White Sox’ Game 2 victory. In addition to emerging as the club’s best starting pitcher in the second half, their only arm trusted to log starter-level innings in the playoffs, Burke has faced the Guardians four times in 2026. In that time, he’s posted a 1.19 ERA, with 27 strikeouts and just four walks in 22 ⅔ innings against them.</p><p>“We have some stuff that we've seen that works, we've got some stuff that we've seen didn't work,” Burke said. “Watch those outings and trying to formulate a plan based off of that.”</p><p>Burke went viral for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/after-a-prospect-path-marked-by-injury-white-sox-starter-sean-burke-is-grateful-for-postseason-opportunity-sam-antonacci-hagen-smith-will-venable-tristan-peters" target="_blank" ><u>comments he made to the Sun-Times</u></a> at the outset of the postseason outlining his singular focus on his craft: “This is my life. I don’t have family, no girl, no kids. This is all I do.”</p><p>In a joking ode to the quote, his teammates have taken to donning shirts that read ‘Celibate for Sean.’</p><p>But rather than a joylessly intense approach that Burke’s remarks might suggest, the 26-year-old carries himself with an ease borne of being freed from the injuries that stalled his prospect rise.</p><p>“I don't really care what any expectations are put on me, not trying to hold myself to any standards,” Burke told the Sun-Times. “I just know I'm good and I want to go out there and just pitch my best every single time, take each game how it is. I feel like I'm a better player in that mindset.</p><p><b>All hands on deck for Game 5</b></p><p>If Burke getting a traditional start rather than an opener suggests that the White Sox will ride him for seven innings, don’t be fooled. White Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b> sounds plenty prepared to aggressively deploy his bullpen in a game where he can’t afford to fall behind.</p><p>“Deciding game here of a series, it's going to be all hands on deck and you kind of throw out the window previous usage,” Venable said. “That is going to take a different level of preparedness and preparation and really just guts and heart.”</p><p><b>Arizona Fall League ranks thinning</b></p><p>Two Sox prospects who are candidates to be major-league camp invites next spring will spend the offseason recovering from surgery rather than continuing to play in the AFL.</p><p>First baseman <b>Anthony DePino</b>, who hit .260/.357/.482 in Double-A this season, underwent a procedure to address a left shoulder/lat injury. Hard-throwing right-handed reliever <b>Pierce George</b>, who struck out 82 in 65 ⅔ innings across four minor league levels this season, suffered an olenacron fracture in his pitching elbow.</p><p>Both are expected to be ready for spring training.</p>

entries.title: John Prine gets star-studded tribute during five days of birthday celebrations
entries.summary: <p>If he was still alive, John Prine, the Maywood mailman turned songwriting hero, would be celebrating his 80th birthday Saturday — and Chicago’s music community didn’t want anyone to forget it.</p><p>Organizers, including Prine’s family, curated a five-day celebration of his life and work that kicked off Oct. 7. Thursday night was the centerpiece, with many luminaries gathering at the Chicago Theatre for a sold-out night of songs and stories that kept all his "Souvenirs" alive.</p><p>“His songs continue to be sung because they reflect the best qualities of people — empathy for the downtrodden, a common-sense approach to living and heartbreak, always followed by a good joke,” said the evening’s host, actor-musician John C. Reilly, kicking off nearly three hours of performances (most of them backed by Prine’s long-time band) that reinvigorated his songbook.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A majority of the performers were notably from Illinois, a decision by organizers to cement Prine’s identity as one of our own. In addition to Steppenwolf alum Reilly, along with Price and half of Wilco, that group also included indie folk-rock group Ratboys who took on “Quiet Man” and country crooner Andrew Sa on “Bad Boy.” The Evanston bluegrass group The Sullivan Sisters joined Chicago banjo player/singer Jonas Friddle on the night’s namesake, “Souvenirs.”</p><p>No reason is ever truly needed to celebrate Illinois’ prodigal music son, who found his tribe in the 1970s Old Town School of Folk Music scene — a mural in his honor was just finished on the exterior of the Lincoln Avenue institute, with artwork from Waco Brothers’ Jon Langford. Langford also appeared Thursday night to offer a pensive “How Lucky Can One Man Get?” and a mural tip for onlookers: “Sneak down the next street [to Oakley] and overlook the Daily Bar to fully see His everyman music extended into his civic work as Prine was a benefactor for many causes related to health care, veteran services, addiction recovery, refugee and immigrant support, and services for the houseless. After Prine died, his family started the <a class="Link" href="https://www.thehellointherefoundation.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Hello in There Foundation</u></a> to continue that work.</p><p>“We want to keep John’s music alive and keep gathering with people, growing the community and donating in his name to people who need it most,” said executive director Celine Thackston, appearing alongside Prine’s wife, Fiona, on stage. Thackston noted the group has donated $1.4 million over the past six years, with proceeds from this week’s events going back to the organization as well.</p><p>Those festivities have included entries.title: Policía fuera de servicio que disparó 2 armas respondía a una llamada por disparos en la casa de su madre
entries.summary: <p>Mientras líderes comunitarios pedían cargos criminales contra un Policía de Chicago acusado de disparar dos armas hacia una calle de La Villita, surgieron nuevos detalles sobre el joven agente fuera de servicio y las circunstancias del tiroteo que hirió a por lo menos un hombre el fin de semana pasado.</p><p>La Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA) identificó al oficial involucrado como Edgar Delgado Arroyo, según un informe obtenido esta semana mediante una solicitud de registros públicos. El reporte de policía señala que no se había presentado ninguna acusación formal contra Delgado Arroyo.</p><p>Una fuente de las autoridades dijo que la policía investiga si hubo un intercambio de disparos después de que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/10/07/policia-de-chicago-fuera-de-servicio-disparo-2-armas-al-mismo-tiempo-que-dejo-heridos-en-la-villita" target="_blank" >el agente abrió fuego inicialmente</a> durante un altercado la madrugada del domingo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-200000" name="module-200000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Delgado Arroyo fue al área después de que su madre reportó que unos disparos anteriores impactaron su casa, según la fuente. Su padre había muerto en un tiroteo cercano en julio de 2021, dijo la fuente.</p><p>Una profunda desconfianza hacia el Departamento de Policía se sintió en el vecindario esta semana, mientras los residentes trataban de reconstruir lo ocurrido y arreglar los daños que quedaron. Una vecina, que pidió no ser identificada por miedo a su seguridad, dijo que un pistolero había “disparado en nuestra casa”.</p><p>“Disparó en un par de casas”, dijo la vecina. “Disparó contra nuestros carros. Sólo estaba disparando de forma imprudente. Y sonaba como si tuviera más de una pistola”.</p><p>La mujer dijo que vio a alguien dar vueltas por la cuadra varias veces antes de entablar conversación con un pequeño grupo reunido frente a su casa y abrir fuego. Cuando fue a la puerta para ver qué pasaba, dijo que escuchó más disparos.</p><p>Al menos otros dos vecinos reportaron que sus casas fueron alcanzadas por los disparos.</p><p>La fuente de las autoridades dijo que los investigadores trabajan para determinar si en algún momento hubo un tiroteo, pero necesitan analizar los casquillos recuperados en la escena. La policía también investiga las trayectorias de las balas que impactaron vehículos para ver si coinciden con la posición del agente durante el tiroteo, dijo la fuente.</p><p>No fue posible localizar a Delgado Arroyo, de 30 años de edad, ni a su abogado.</p><p>Los registros policiales muestran que Delgado Arroyo ingresó a la academia de policía como recluta en noviembre de 2023 y ahora gana un salario anual de $100,950. La policía dijo que está asignado al Distrito Grand Crossing y que fue puesto en labores administrativas por 30 días después del tiroteo.</p><p>Antes había sido mencionado en una queja disciplinaria que fue cerrada administrativamente, según la oficina del inspector general del Ayuntamiento. Ahora enfrenta investigaciones que podrían llevar a una remisión por cargos criminales, según un portavoz de la fiscalía estatal del Condado de Cook.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Comunitario de La Villita ofreció una conferencia de prensa el jueves por la tarde para plantear preguntas sobre el tiroteo y “exigir” cargos. Leonardo Quintero, miembro del concejo policial del distrito vecino preguntó por qué el agente no fue detenido.</p><p>“A la policía se supone que se le da un poder extraordinario”, dijo Quintero a los periodistas. “Eso significa que también debe estar sujeta a una rendición de cuentas extraordinaria”.</p><p></p><h3>El altercado derivó en disparos</h3><p>Los oficiales reportaron un tiroteo cerca de las calles 24th y Rockwell alrededor de las 12:45 a.m. del domingo, según grabaciones de la radio policial. Habían sido llamados al área una hora antes por otro reporte de disparos.</p><p>Una despachadora alertó a los oficiales de que vio en una cámara al tirador de pie detrás de una SUV con una pistola en la mano, según una grabación. Segundos después, otro llamado reportó a una persona baleada a mitad de cuadra.</p><p>Los oficiales encontraron al presunto tirador y confirmaron que era un policía fuera de servicio que había recibido un golpe en la cara y sangraba del ojo izquierdo, según el tráfico radial. Un oficial informó que el policía fuera de servicio no había recibido un disparo y luego añadió que había “pandilleros en la cuadra”.</p><p>La fuente de las autoridades dijo que Delgado Arroyo estaba hablando por teléfono con el 911 cuando fue golpeado y luego abrió fuego.</p><p>En una declaración el martes, COPA dijo que el agente involucrado en el tiroteo iba conduciendo cuando se encontró con un grupo en la cuadra, pero la agencia de supervisión no identificó públicamente al oficial. Intercambió palabras con un hombre y luego disparó un arma “varias veces”, dijo COPA.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure La ubicación del incidente queda confirmada en el informe que identifica a Delgado Arroyo como el oficial involucrado.</p><p>Un hombre recibió dos impactos y fue llevado al Hospital Mount Sinai en condición estable, dijo la policía. La fuente lo describió como un hombre de 24 años vinculado a la pandilla callejera Satan’s Disciples.</p><p>La policía primero se refirió a él como un “ofensor”, diciendo que golpeó en la cara al policía fuera de servicio durante la discusión. COPA no repitió esa afirmación.</p><p>Fue puesto bajo custodia y luego liberado, según la policía. El portavoz de la fiscalía estatal dijo que la policía nunca contactó a su unidad de revisión de delitos graves para revisar posibles cargos.</p><p>El agente y un segundo hombre también fueron hospitalizados por lesiones, informaron las autoridades.</p><p>Baltazar Enríquez, presidente del Concilio Comunitario de La Villita, dijo que quiere que el agente y otros policías que puedan vivir en el vecindario entiendan que “no están por encima de la ley”.</p><p>“No necesitamos vaqueros”, dijo al Chicago Sun-Times. “Necesitamos oficiales”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Citywide expansion of automated bus, bike lane violation program advances in City Council panel
entries.summary: <p>A City City council panel has advanced a measure to expand a program that automates enforcement of parking violations in bus and bike lanes.</p><p>The city's nearly 2-year-old Smart Streets pilot would grow in phases to cover the entire city in 2028, according to the ordinance backed Friday by the Council’s Committee on Pedestrian and Traffic Safety.</p><p>The pilot is currently limited to a handful of ticket-issuing, camera-equipped Department of Finance vehicles and CTA buses. The current boundaries are North Avenue, Ashland Avenue, Roosevelt Road and Lake Michigan.</p><p>The ordinance would expand those boundaries, and the number of vehicles with cameras, if passed at next week's City Council meeting.</p><p>The CTA expects to add cameras to 52 total buses in the next couple of weeks, Molly Poppe, CTA’s chief planning and innovation officer, told the committee. The ordinance lets the CTA add cameras to 100 buses total.</p><p>The Department of Finance would expand its camera-equipped vehicle fleet from eight to 26, Chuck Billow, the department's deputy director of street operations, told the committee. If the program expands next year, the city could expect 207,000 parking violations and $9.4 million of increased gross revenue.</p><p>The program's boundaries would be expanded twice before going citywide, he said. The first phase would happen in January, when the boundaries would grow to Foster Avenue, California Avenue and Pershing Road. In July, the boundaries would grow to Devon Avenue, Pulaski Road and 51st Street. The program would go citywide in January 2028.</p><p>Committee Chair Daniel La Spata (1st) said the pilot program, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/11/04/smart-streets-bus-bike-lane-ticket" target="_blank" >kicked off</a> in 2024 after more than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/07/10/automated-ticketing-cameras-traffic-crosswalks-loading-zones-bus-bike-lanes-council-committee" target="_blank" >a year and a half of delays</a>, has already shown it is discouraging drivers from illegally parking in bike and bus lanes. He said 82% of drivers who received a warning never got a ticket. And 62% of motorists who got a ticket did not get a second ticket, he said.</p><p>Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th), the measure's sponsor, said the idea for expanding parking enforcement began in 2022 after several children were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/6/22/23179365/neighbors-gather-mourn-lincoln-square-toddler-killed-car-push-cyclist-safety-measures" target="_blank" >fatally struck</a> by drivers.</p>
entries.author: David Struett

entries.title: 1985 Bears championship team remembers former coach Mike Ditka as 'tip of the spear'
entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka’s former players have seemingly endless stories that capture the essence of who he was as a coach and a man. Those memories returned in a rush Friday when Ditka, who led <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> to their only Super Bowl and towered as a Chicago icon, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" target="_blank" >died at 86</a>.</p><p>Hall of Fame defensive lineman Dan Hampton’s snapshot might speak the loudest, especially as the Bears are set to visit the archrival Packers on Sunday.</p><p>The teams actually played a preseason game against each other in 1984 at Milwaukee County Stadium. Logistics were challenging since it was a baseball facility, and both teams were on the same sideline. So Ditka stood at one 49-yard line and Packers coach Forrest Gregg stood at the other, and Ditka spent the entire game screaming profanities at his counterpart.</p><p>“He was the tip of the spear,” Hampton told the Sun-Times. “A lot of coaches say, ‘OK, do this, do this,’ and then they stand back and watch. Ditka was right there at the front.</p><p>“It was about us against you. Our team against you. Let’s go. It didn’t matter that it was preseason to Ditka.”</p><p>Ditka coached the Bears to a five-year run as the NFL’s most powerful force as they went 62-17 from 1984 through ’88, the peak being his 1985 championship team that won Super Bowl XX. It is the only Lombardi Trophy in franchise history, and no coach since has matched his dominance.</p><p>Playing for him was grueling, so much so that Hall of Fame linebacker Mike Singletary referred to him as “a real badass,” but it brought out their best. They learned the value of preparation, they worked relentlessly and they adopted his relentless ferocity.</p><p>“I didn’t realize how wonderful it was to be able to play for him until years after I retired and I got to see the full scope of all these different coaches,” Hampton said. “Nothing felt better than if we were playing against the 49ers and we go out and execute and we beat their ass, and then come into the locker room and he was like a proud father.”</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Judge orders woman detained in killing of 7-year-old, saying she's 'as dangerous as a person can be'
entries.summary: <p>A woman accused of fatally stabbing a 7-year-old girl was ordered detained Friday as the girl’s loved ones packed a Cook County courtroom for an initial hearing that centered on the brutal attack and the defendant’s history of severe mental illness.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Judge John Hock found that Shavon Gayden was “as dangerous as a person can be,” then ordered her held in the Cook County Jail. Gayden, 48, faces one count of first-degree murder in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/vigil-held-for-7-year-old-girl-killed-in-chatham-stabbing" target="_blank" >death of Eddimar Hernández-Chacón</a> last week.</p><p>Eddimar’s family donned shirts emblazoned with her picture and listened closely as prosecutors described the “brutal and evil attack on a 7-year-old child.”</p><p>Eddimar and her older sister were walking in the 8600 block of South Cottage Grove around noon on Oct. 3 when Gayden began jogging toward them with her arm raised, Assistant State’s Attorney Mike Pekara said in court Friday.</p><p>Gayden first lunged toward the sister, then grabbed Eddimar, pulled her to the ground and began stabbing her, Pekara said.</p><p>The sister screamed out for help as Eddimar fell into her arms and Gayden walked away from the scene, according to Pekara. Eddimar suffered four stab wounds to her back and was pronounced dead at Comer Children’s Hospital soon after.</p><p>Three of Gayden’s four previous arrests also involved knives, according to Pekara and court records.</p><p>Before Saturday’s attack, Gayden was inside a store on Cottage Grove Avenue trying to pay her cellphone bill when she became “impatient” with the workers and threatened to stab one in the neck, Pekara said.</p><p>“The knife is her instrument of death, it's her instrument of violence, it's her instrument of assault,’ Pekara said. “The violence that she visited upon that child it was … unpredictable”</p><p>Hock ordered Gayden detained pending trial on Friday, citing her violent background and “severe mental health issues.” He also ordered a psychiatric evaluation. </p><p>“She's shown now she will attack and potentially kill one of the most vulnerable members of our society,” Hock said. “She is as dangerous as a person can be, very likely due to serious mental health issues.”</p><p>Gayden’s attorney, Assistant Public Defender Brett Balmer, didn’t oppose Pekara’s petition for detention. Balmer told the court she agreed that Gayden needed to remain in custody and under the care of a doctor.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> homelessness.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“She obviously is not in any condition to be released on the street,” Balmer told reporters after court. “As I indicated on Monday, she is in the middle of a severe psychiatric crisis and needs help.”</p><p>Balmer said her client has struggled with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/07/shavon-gayden-eddimar-hernandez-chacon-murder-chicago-crime" target="_blank" >mental illness</a> and homelessness, noting that Gayden “was living on the street." But Balmer pushed back on prosecutors' characterization of Gayden as “evil.”</p><p>“I would counter by saying she's mentally ill,” Balmer said. “Those are not synonymous. I have dealt with a lot of mentally ill clients with very very horrible cases, like this one. It is tragic. It is heartbreaking.”</p><p>Gayden’s mental health began deteriorating about a decade ago, but she “never received the psychiatric care she needed,” according to Balmer. </p><p>In 2016, Gayden was arrested for stabbing her boyfriend with a “small knife,” according to Pekara. She was arrested again in 2019 for running toward her son with a knife. Both cases were dismissed after the victims failed to appear in court.</p><p>Gayden was then charged with striking a Chicago Transit Authority employee in 2023 and threatening to stab her, court records show. Three knives were recovered from her purse. She later pleaded guilty to those charges in 2024 and received probation for two years.</p><p>About a month after her plea deal, she was arrested again for attacking a shelter worker. Gayden then stopped showing up to court in the CTA case, and a warrant was issued for her arrest last year, according to court records. The warrant was still active when she was arrested Saturday.</p><p>Balmer said Gayden’s mother is devastated by what happened “at the hands of her daughter.” Gayden’s mother has repeatedly said “this would not have happened" if her daughter had just received the help she needed, according to Balmer.</p><p>“I believe she used the words ‘ticking time bomb,'" Balmer added.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/vigil-held-for-7-year-old-girl-killed-in-chatham-stabbing" >Woman charged in killing of 7-year-old girl has history of jarring attacks</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/07/shavon-gayden-eddimar-hernandez-chacon-murder-chicago-crime" >Mental health system failed woman accused of fatally stabbing 7-year-old girl, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka, one of the most iconic players and coaches in the history of the Chicago Bears, died Friday at age 86. entries.title: Hotel workers strike ahead of Chicago marathon, seek better pay and benefits
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of Chicago hotel workers walked off the job Friday at six downtown hotels to demand wage increases, better benefits and safer workloads as thousands of visitors arrive for marathon weekend.</p><p>Workers have been negotiating new contracts for four months, after their previous agreements expired Aug. 31. Karen Kent, president of UNITE HERE Local 1, a hospitality workers union, said negotiations have made limited progress and workers are struggling to afford basic expenses.</p><p>“People have reported going to food banks, taking payday loans to pay their rent and pay their bills,” Kent said.</p><p>The workers are employed at the Millennium Hotel Knickerbocker Chicago, Palmer House Hilton, Sheraton Grand Chicago Riverwalk, Waldorf Astoria Chicago, The Westin Chicago River North and The Westin Michigan Avenue Chicago. This weekend, hotels, including these, are expecting thousands of visitors arriving to the city as 75% of the Bank of America Chicago Marathon's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-marathon/why-runners-participate-history" >more than 55,000 participants</a> travel from outside of Illinois.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams practices for 1st time since injury
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams is back ... at practice,</p><p>Almost three weeks after pulling his hamstring in a loss to the Vikings, Williams participated in practice for the first time Friday. During the portion of practice open to the media, he stretched and jogged across the field with his fellow quarterbacks. Friday is the lightest of the Bears' three practice days, and Williams was limited. </p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson has already called Tyson Bagent his starter for the rivalry game. The Bears listed Williams as questionable to play.</p><p>The Bears play in Atlanta the following Sunday. </p><p>Johnson called Williams' return date "to be determined."</p><p>Williams threw to teammates on Wednesday after practice as part of his return-to-play progression.</p><p>"We’ve got him progressively increasing the amount of running that’s going on — and of course the throwing aspect of it is a big part of his position as well," Johnson said before Friday's practice. "Our guys have a good plan in place and we’re just going step by step with that right now and every couple of days we’re getting a throwing protocol in and making sure there are no setbacks. So far so good."<br></p>

entries.title: Packers praise Mike Ditka as 'one of the fiercest competitors in NFL history'
entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka earned some grudging respect from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' rivals on Friday.</p><p>Shortly after his death, the Packers put out a statement praising the Hall of Fame tight end and iconoclast coach.</p><p>"One of the fiercest competitors in NFL history, Mike helped define the intensity and tradition of the Packers-Bears rivalry, the oldest in professional football," a statement from the Packers read. "He embodied the toughness and passion that have made the rivalry one of the most storied in all of sports.</p><p>"While he was a formidable opponent, his contributions to the game and to a rivalry that has meant so much to both franchises will always be respected and remembered by the Green Bay Packers."</p><p>The Packers figure to acknowledge Ditka's death at Lambeau Field on Sunday before the teams line up for the 214th playing of the rivalry game. The Bears are likely to add a helmet sticker or jersey patch in Ditka's honor, too.</p>

entries.title: 'It's terrible,' says mom of CTA janitor slain during shift at Near West Side L station
entries.summary: <p>Screams. That is how Joyce Mobley learned of her son Julian Mobley’s stabbing death.</p><p>It happened while he was working as a janitor at the Near West Side’s Damen Avenue Green Line station — coming to the aid of another staffer who’d gotten pepper-sprayed. </p><p>Joyce Mobley's daughter was in another room and had taken a call from Julian’s wife. “I could hear my daughter in the front bedroom screaming," Joyce Mobley said. “That’s how I got the news.”</p><p>Hardly able to hold on to the steering wheel, Joyce Mobley drove to Stroger Hospital to see her 41-year-old son.</p><p>“It’s terrible," she said, adding that the only solace she has found is the thought of him resting after enduring such pain during the attack that reportedly occurred <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/08/man-fatally-stabbed-during-argument-at-cta-station-on-near-west-side" target="_blank" >at 3 p.m. at the Damen Green Line station, 154 N. Damen Ave.</a> </p><p> “It helps my heart. I know he’s at peace because he’s asleep. Now he’s OK,” she said.</p><p>The attack unfolded as the suspect, who is now in police custody after turning himself in, began to fight with another CTA worker, possibly a conductor, said Julian's mom. </p><p>Julian, who witnessed the fight, had turned his back to help the staffer, who couldn’t see after having been pepper-sprayed by the suspect. That's when the suspect, brandishing what appeared to be scissors, stabbed Julian in the back of his neck, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. </p><p>Julian then "ran around the courtyard of the station and went inside of his utility room," where firefighters and paramedics from Ambulance 53 found him, the report said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital in "very critical condition," but he was pronounced dead a short time later. A Friday autopsy determined he died of a stab wound to his neck, and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>“It was a natural reaction. He was trying to help his co-worker clear his eyes," said Joyce Mobley, who was told that her son was trying to render aid before being stabbed. “He turned his back on the perpetrator. He didn’t think the perpetrator was upset with him,” his mom said. “That’s inhumane." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure where he lived with his wife and two kids. They had a close-knit family, with many aunts and uncles and a small circle of good friends. </p><p>He was one of four Mobley siblings — three boys and a girl, said his mom, who added the siblings are all adults now.</p><p>He attended Hyde Park Academy High School at 6220 S. Stony Island Ave. until being forced to leave because of bullying, his mom said. </p><p>Julian was 14 years older than one of his brothers, and he took pride in being a big brother.</p><p>“He was kinda bossy,” his mother joked.</p><p>Lately, he had only wanted to spend more time with his family and his brother, whom he'd started working out with at L.A. Fitness after shifts at the CTA. He’d worked at CTA since 2018. </p><p>“He was hardworking, and he was a kind man,” his mom said. “A friendly man.”</p><p>Julian changed his diet and started taking vitamins, his mom recalled. “He came to understand he had to eat a certain way to gain weight,” his mom said.</p><p>His family had been looking forward to another trip to Disney World in Orlando, Florida, and Julian was saving money for it. Earlier, he had taken his 14-year-old daughter, but this time he wanted to go as a family, including their new baby and 1-year-old boy. “They were saving money for the future," she said.</p><p>Stricken with grief, Joyce Mobley is also disturbed by the feelings of worry.</p><p>“It just makes me worry about everyone’s life because it could have happened to any one of us." </p><p>In a statement, the transit agency offered condolences:</p><p>“We will support law enforcement officials’ efforts to ensure that the offender is apprehended and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”</p><p>Julian was mild-mannered and kind, and his eyes lit up when he talked about his children, according to rail janitor and Local 308 union board member Audrey Veasley.</p><p>“He was a gentleman,” Veasley said during a news conference hours after the incident. “He was a real man.”</p><p>No charges have been announced. </p>

entries.title: Brothers navigate White Sox emotional roller coaster. A game at Rate Field 'makes us feel connected'
entries.summary: <p>Daniel Zoric and his younger brother, Charlie, were bound by their White Sox fandom before they shared the same air.</p><p>Daniel, 24, has been a fan for as long as he walked this earth. But 20-year-old Charlie's fandom began before he was born. When their mom was pregnant with Charlie, she attended Game 2 of the 2005 World Series between the Sox and Houston Astros.</p><p>“It’s always been like a running joke in our family that [Charlie’s] been to a World Series game and I haven’t,” Daniel said.</p><p>“I tease him about it every chance I get,” said Charlie with a wide grin.</p><p>The brothers attended their first Sox postseason game together Thursday night, and though the team fell to the Cleveland Guardians 9-5 to send the series to a decisive winner-take-all game in Cleveland Saturday night, Daniel and Charlie forged memories that they’ll carry together for years.</p><p>They’ve lost count of how many hours they’ve spent at Sox games side by side, but Thursday was the first Sox postseason game that they attended together.</p><p>Daniel and Charlie grew up on baseball fields, whether it was at Sox home games through their parents' shared love for the team or at Daniel’s organized baseball games.</p><p>The brothers, driving in from Western Springs, wanted to bask in the postseason festivities Thursday, starting with a tailgate in Lot C in front of their Mazda CX-5 over four hours before game time.</p><p>While a select few fans, including Daniel, were slightly nervous going into Thursday night’s game, a vast majority were confident, including Charlie.</p><p>“I think the team can do it given how easy it was [in] their first two games away,” Charlie said. “They had to lose a game at some point, it may as well be when they’re playing people they’ve played in their division, instead of playing the Rays.”</p><p>Daniel believed the Sox playing a division rival they’d seen several times this season was a potential weakness.</p><p>“They know us better than anyone else,” that’s my only concern,” Daniel said. </p><p>“I’m a little nervous but I have faith,” Daniel added, before Charlie immediately jumped in declaring that he “had no nerves.”</p><p>The brothers passed time by talking about sports and bets.</p><p>"This will pay for our tickets," Daniel, who paid $100 for tickets near left field, said as he fist-bumped his brother after spending several minutes talking about a bet he wanted to place. After entering the stadium, the brothers took a lap around the stadium’s concourse — a tradition they typically do when at Sox games.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div jabs about Charlie’s “World Series appearance,” Daniel playfully fired back at his brother during the first inning.</p><p>“So far, way better atmosphere than yesterday, I mean you don’t know that, but I do,” Daniel told Charlie.</p><p>By the end of the third inning, Daniel and Charlie were singing, cheering and, Charlie said, “feeling electric,” after the Sox jumped to an early 2-0 lead. Daniel was constantly texting his dad about how the game was going.</p><p>When asked what the emotions have been like since the first pitch, Daniel gestured in the motion of a roller coaster.</p><p>“Up and down the whole time,” he said as the game moved toward the middle innings.</p><p>By the bottom of the sixth, Daniel and Charlie’s demeanor — along with much of the Sox faithful — had drastically changed after Cleveland scored six times to go up 9-4.</p><p>“We still got a shot,” the brothers said, not nearly as enthusiastic as they were earlier in the game. “There’s still a lot of baseball left.”</p><p>By the end of the eighth, the brothers had seen enough and decided it was time to leave.</p><p>After the Sox appeared to threaten a rally in the ninth inning, Daniel scrambled to turn the game on over the radio as Rate Field grew farther in his rear view mirror.</p><p>When a lineout to left field ended the game, he quickly switched the station off.</p><p>“The hope was there,” Daniel said between laughs.</p><p>Despite the deflating loss, Daniel and Charlie had a good laugh over biting into the wrappers of the Jimmy John sandwiches they had saved for hours.</p><p>Win or lose, the two agreed that their love for the team keeps their bond close.</p><p>“It makes us feel — ” Daniel said and Charlie interjected “connected.”</p>

entries.title: The times when fiery Mike Ditka lost his cool, threatening fans, his boss and the media
entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka told it like it was — and Chicago loved him for it. No beating around the bush, but maybe a threat to beat the bejesus out of someone who got his goat. Whether it was an obnoxious Bears fan yelling at him after a loss on the field or a reporter who asked a question he didn’t care to answer, Da Coach always had a ready, blunt and frequently hilarious response.</p><h3>Threatening Neal from North Lake </h3><p>In 1992, Ditka had a weekly show on WSCR-AM Radio. A caller accused the Bears coach of being a crybaby. Ditka promptly offered to meet the caller, “Neal from North Lake,” at the coach’s downtown office at a time of Neal’s choosing. “You tell me what time and when, and I’ll whip your ass,” the 53-year-old coach said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lLJeRB0saww?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Mike Ditka Challenges A Caller "Neal From North Lake" On His Weekly Radio Show (November 2, 1992)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Throwing his gum at a Niners fan</h3><p>It wasn’t just punches that Ditka threw or threatened to throw. In 1987, after his team suffered a 41-0 loss in San Francisco, Ditka hurled a wad of gum into the stands, allegedly hitting a woman. During the game, fans had been throwing beer and ice cubes at the Bears bench.</p><p>"Any time someone throws something at me," he later said, "I'm going to throw it back."</p><h3>Ditka’s press conferences</h3><p>Ditka was often at his fiery best during press conferences, especially when things weren’t going so well for his team, like when this reporter asked Ditka why he was in such a bad mood.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@nflonfox/video/7209088604084260139" data-video-id="7209088604084260139" data-embed-from="oembed" style="max-width:605px; min-width:325px;"> <section> <a target="_blank" title="@nflonfox" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@nflonfox?refer=embed">@nflonfox</a> <p>Never gets old 😂 <a title="mikeditka" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/mikeditka?refer=embed">#mikeditka</a> <a title="chicagobears" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/chicagobears?refer=embed">#chicagobears</a> <a title="nfl" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/nfl?refer=embed">#nfl</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> </p> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - NFLonFOX" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7209088625512942382?refer=embed">♬ original sound - NFLonFOX</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div></div><p>On one occasion, Ditka all but abandoned his press duties (at least for a time) to spar with a heckling passerby. “I’d rather talk to him,” Ditka told reporters. “I know I’m smarter than that son of a b---h.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/KktJbYw8ppY?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago Bears Legend Mike Ditka telling a heckler he has a IQ of zero. #chicagobears"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Ditka challenging the Bears fan base for sitting on their hands</h3><p>Even after a Bears win, Ditka was more than happy to berate fans who he thought didn’t do enough to support their team: “I thought we were in a mortuary for a while.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9HjOQT2phzw?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Mike Ditka Raps Bears Fans for Sitting on Their Hands"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>When Ditka took on George Halas</h3><p>Almost anyone was fair game in Ditka’s book. When he was a tight end for the Bears, got traded to the Philadelphia Eagles in 1967, he famously said: Owner George Halas “throws nickels around like manhole covers.” </p><p>Ditka, on the occasion of having his jersey retired in 2013, told the Sun-Times: “I think it hurt him. It bothered him, even though I said it in jest. I said it as a joke at a banquet, trying to be a smart ass, like we all are. But I think it bothered him, I really do. And I told him that I never really meant it that way. But then again, he forgot about it because he hired me as a coach. But at that time, it did bother him. Don’t forget, that was the sixties. There was no big money being made in pro football, believe me.”</p><h3>Ditka and Buddy Ryan </h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/L6NZK5t8Fso?si=KVRsexKDAcyXGDs3" target="_blank" >They feuded for years</a> and famously shoved each other during half-time of the Bears’ only defeat of the 1985 season, a 38-24 loss to the Dolphins. Ditka was the head coach, Buddy Ryan, his defensive coordinator. But when Ryan died in 2016, Ditka had mostly kind things to say about his former rival: “Buddy and I, we were good for each other,” Ditka told the Sun-Times, “because we were good for the Bears.”<br></p>
entries.author: Stefano Esposito

entries.title: Where have all the White Sox' home runs gone?
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — In August 2022, then-White Sox general manager Rick Hahn was discussing the team’s lack of power when he summed up the effect the long ball can have.</p><p>“Ball goes far, team goes far,” he said.</p><p>The ball did not go far for the Sox that season. They finished 10th in the American League with 149 homers, 21 below the league average. They also finished 81-81 and missed the playoffs.</p><p>In 2026, the Sox hit 211 homers, the third-most homers in the league, went 84-78 and made the playoffs. Granted, it was a down year for the league, but the production helps prove a point. Let’s not nitpick here.</p><p>Home-run power carried the Sox’ offense this season. Munetaka Murakami (35), Miguel Vargas (33) and Colson Montgomery (31) each hit 30 homers, becoming the fourth trio in Sox history to do it and the first since 2008 — Carlos Quentin (36), Jermaine Dye (34) and Jim Thome (34).</p><p>But in the American League Division Series against the Guardians — which will conclude Saturday night with Game 5 — the Sox have a mere two home runs. Murakami hit a monster two-run homer in the fourth inning of Game 1 that led to a Sox victory, and Vargas hit a solo shot in a Game 4 loss with the Sox trailing by five in the ninth.</p><p>Where have all the homers gone?</p><p>“I think that we’re facing really good pitchers, No. 1,” Sox manager Will Venable said Friday before the team departed for Cleveland. “Whatever we want to say about some of the chase that we’ve seen, I think at the end of the day, we’re facing really good pitchers that are executing well, making it really hard for us, like they have all year.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/09/white-sox-disappointed-but-not-dismayed-as-they-head-back-to-cleveland-for-do-or-die-game-5" >White Sox disappointed, but not dismayed as they head back to Cleveland for do-or-die Game 5</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/10/09/white-sox-right-hander-sean-burke-tabbed-to-start-do-or-die-alds-game-5-sean-burke-will-venable" >White Sox right-hander Sean Burke tabbed to start do-or-die ALDS Game 5</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Indeed, against division opponents in the regular season, the Sox hit their fewest homers against the Guardians (16 in 13 games).</p><p>“You have to give those guys some credit,” Venable said. “Our hitters, you see some guys that are still in really good spots. We’ve had some good at-bats, just not the slug we've seen throughout the year. But in the playoffs, things are different.”</p><p>Boy, are they. On Thursday, the Sox faced eight pitchers, none for more than 2 ⅓ innings. In Game 3, Murakami faced four and Vargas five. In the series, Murakami has faced nine pitchers and Vargas 10. It’s all about matchups in the playoffs, and the Guardians are winning those.</p><p>“It is tough to face a lot of different pitchers,” the left-handed-hitting Tristan Peters, who has seen his share of lefties, said Thursday. “But at the same time, I think we’ve put some good at-bats together. We’re just going to have to grind through that.”</p><p>“I thought some at-bats we bounced back, had some good little runs there and just couldn’t get that big hit,” Chase Meidroth said. “But they’re a great pitching staff, so it’s not easy. It’s not easy against them ever.”</p><p>To be sure, Murakami and Vargas have been productive. Murakami has an .820 OPS, and Vargas is at 1.367. But the Sox’ overall OPS is .622, down more than 100 points from their regular-season mark of .726.</p><p>“We have to find different ways,” Venable said. “We've done a really good job — yesterday was a great example — of really grinding. We're grinding offensively to do whatever we can to score runs, whether that’s via the homer or not.</p><p>The Guardians — who ranked 13th in home runs in the AL during the regular season with 162 — didn’t go deep in the series until Thursday, when Patrick Bailey and a rejuvenated Jose Ramirez homered. So after being separated by 49 homers over six months, the teams are even through four games. Such is playoff baseball.</p><p>“Obviously, slug has been part of our identity and something that we’ve done in the postseason,” said Venable, whose team hit two homers in the two-game wild-card series. “You have to find different ways. Pitchers are so good that you hope that you can get a guy on and hit one out of the ballpark. Hopefully that happens for us in Game 5.”</p><p>Righty Gavin Williams is set to start for the Guardians. He lasted a whopping five innings in Game 2, which the Sox rallied to win. Considering he also pitched the ninth inning Thursday, perhaps the Sox have gotten enough of a look at him to take advantage of him. But with 10 other guys ready to go, it might not matter.</p><p>As Venable said, the playoffs are different.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Willis Tower turns navy and orange after Mike Ditka's death
entries.summary: <p>The Willis Tower antenna will be lit in navy and orange Friday night in tribute to former coach Mike Ditka, who died earlier in the day.</p><p>The skyscraper's web site announced the decision. Willis Tower typically lights up for special events, causes and tributes.</p><p>Ditka died at age 86 around 9 a.m. Friday. </p><p>"Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever," his family said in a statement.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson, Bears players and NFL luminaries honored Ditka throughout the day Friday. Johnson called him the "gold standard" inside Halas Hall. His No. 89 was the last retired by the Bears.</p><p>The Bears, in a statement, said that "Mike's impact on the Chicago Bears organization, over decades as a player, coach and proud icon and ambassador for our organization, is immeasurable." </p><p>The Bears, who are 3-1 this season. play the rival Packers at Lambeau Field on Sunday at noon.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Mayor Johnson uses 4th veto to kill debt threshold measure, setting stage for override vote next week
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Friday used his fourth veto to try to bury <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-raises-debt-threshold-marty-quinn-mayor-brandon-johnson" >an ordinance</a> that would make it more difficult to issue city debt by raising the threshold for City Council approval to 30 votes, setting the stage for an attempt at an override. </p><p>“Neighborhoods with the greatest infrastructure needs should not face additional barriers to securing essential public investment,” Johnson wrote in his veto letter to the city clerk.</p><p>“Delaying infrastructure projects can increase construction costs, worsen deterioration and ultimately cost taxpayers more. While this ordinance increases a voting threshold, it does not put into place any additional measures around debt affordability, reporting requirement or financial oversight." </p><p>The mayor also said that the three-fifths vote requirement is higher than the 26 votes needed to approve the city’s $16.6 billion budget “or any other critical matter that comes before this body."</p><p>The veto has been expected ever since the 32 to 15 vote on Sept. 29 that Johnson has insinuated had racial motives — by branding the reform championed by retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) a “three-fifths compromise.” The same term is used to describe language in the Constitution that originally counted Black slaves as three-fifths of a person. Several Black Council members, including Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell, voted for Quinn's measure.</p><p>Quinn said at that meeting that he expected a veto, and that the 34 votes he would need for an override of a veto was "a reach.” He has already failed once when Johnson vetoed an ordinance that would have banned the sale of hemp.</p><p>But Quinn said Friday he would try for an override anyway, and focus his efforts on three Council members who ducked out before the roll call on Sept. 29: Alds. Daniel La Spata (1st); Chris Taliaferro (29th) and Andre Vasquez (40th).</p><p>In a text to the Sun-Times, Vasquez said his office is “in negotiation to establish more transparency and accountability as it relates to bonds and borrowing without needing to lift the threshold to 30” votes.</p><p>“We have been in discussions this week and will do so over the weekend to see if agreement can be found,” Vasquez said. “The results of those conversations will inform whether I vote to sustain the veto or not.”</p><p>Taliaferro told the Sun-Times he was considering the issue, adding, ”After I get an opportunity to speak to the mayor and speak to my colleagues, I’ll make a decision on whether or not to support a veto.”</p><p>LaSpata said, “I don’t have a public comment at the moment but I will speak to it in Council.”</p><p>Quinn learned how to count votes while working alongside his political mentor, now convicted former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan. He knows how difficult it will be to sway mayoral allies who took a pass the first time around. But Quinn said he would try because “the policy is solid,” the city’s crushing “debt level is real and what we pay in debt payments is real.”</p><p></p><p>“The mayor is pushing back against Council independence. I’m not surprised," Quinn said. "A lot of his actions defy logic. But I will be full steam ahead. If alders want to side with him on this issue, that may be ill-advised because the taxpayers of the city of Chicago don’t trust him with the checkbook.”</p><p>According to the Civic Federation, the city’s outstanding net debt rose by 32.8%, from $22 billion to $29.2 billion, between 2014 and 2023 — an amount driven by increased O’Hare Airport debt that was retired by airline revenue.</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson said the override vote would be “inextricably intertwined with budget objections of individual alders, and I expect that would be part of the play here in the determination as to whether or not there would be an override.”</p><p>But with 40% of Chicago’s operating budget gobbled up by pension and debt payments, Ferguson was unequivocal in his support for raising the bar before issuing even more debt.</p><p>“Our debt is one of the huge legacy issues that is a millstone around the city’s current fiscal situation,” Ferguson said Friday. “Recent debt issuance practices suggest a serious drift back to the worst of our practices. Kicking the can down the road. Delaying payments in schedules that places the primary burden on our children and grandchildren. A continuation of that are the very signals that may be the tipping point with respect to the rating agencies.”</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: White Sox disappointed, but not dismayed as they head back to Cleveland for do-or-die Game 5
entries.summary: <p>In the hushed environs of a post-playoff loss clubhouse, as White Sox players are asked how they can possibly get themselves ready to win a do-or-die Game 5 in Cleveland after a pair of devastating home defeats, there are reminders that this is a game played largely by 20-somethings.</p><p>“We’ve got to get on an airplane,” deadpanned outfielder Sam Antonacci. “That’s what it takes to get there.”</p><p>The locker room atmosphere in the wake of the Sox spurning an opportunity to clinch a postseason series in front of their fans for the first time in 120 years wasn’t happy or glib. But if the two members of their position player core whose on-field demeanors are most likely to be described as “intense,” “scary,” or “scary intense,” were immediately putting things in perspective, dented morale isn’t the great challenge the White Sox face to reach the American League Championship Series.</p><p>“We get more baseball, not everyone gets that,” second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “Nobody thought ‘Maybe this will go 3-0,’ no shot. Those guys can baseball and so can we. It’s a dogfight and everyone knew that coming into it.”</p><p>If anything, the Sox spent their doomed homestand assuring that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/17/miguel-vargas-white-sox-dont-mind-playing-from-behind-we-like-being-the-underdog-sean-burke-colson-montgomery-luis-castillo-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>their season-long preference for playing from behind</u></a>, or defying expectations, wouldn’t hamper their efforts to close out the ALDS while comfortably ahead. Now playing a win-or-go-home game in hostile territory, they are back to standard operating procedure.</p><p>“We’ve shown that all year,” said outfielder Tristan Peters. “We’ve lost games, and we come right back. You just can’t dwell on these kinds of losses. All you can do is look forward.”</p><p>Besides, anyone can see the White Sox’ issues are more tangible. Rookie Hagen Smith, pitching on back-to-back days, couldn’t throw enough strikes to complete the first inning on Thursday night. Grant Taylor, stretched to new lengths all postseason, didn’t allow much hard contact while failing to retire any of the six batters he faced. But 18 pitches from Taylor without a swinging strike is a red flag of its own.</p><p>The Sox have relied on bullpen games in the name of leaning on their strengths, but to the point that their relievers are no longer an available strength. Game 5 starter Sean Burke is fully rested, but was in the bullpen during Game 4 preparing to pitch had the Sox come back.</p><p>“There's only so many guys on our roster,” said manager Will Venable. “We’ve got outs to get and we gotta go with the guys you think would be the best chance to do it.”</p><p>That’s not the most encouraging status report for the freshness of White Sox arms. But it would be a mistake to gawk at the pitching resources exhausted by Venable and ignore the measures Guardians manager Stephen Vogt took to catch him.</p><p>Game 5 starter Gavin Williams threw 18 pitches to get the last three outs on Thursday, which the Guardians have sold as just a more intense version of his mid-week bullpen, but is something the right-hander has never done before two days a start in his pro career. Cleveland’s five-best relief arms have all worked three times or more already, with Hunter Gaddis and All-Star closer Cade Smith working each game of the series.</p><p>“When you have to play three-straight elimination games, there's going to be some high volume,” Vogt said. “There's going to be some unorthodox things that need to happen.”</p><p>If recent White Sox history is a lesson, maybe nothing can protect them from annihilation if Guardians third baseman Jose Ramirez, troubled by his aching left wrist for most of the year, is as fully operational as his last two games suggest. But in measuring out how both teams have wrung out their bullpens like a wet towel for the last four games, it matches what the ALDS series standings already shows.</p><p>For better or worse, they’re even.</p><p>“Good pitching, good lineups,” Burke said. “I think we match up.”</p>

entries.title: Man who punched bank executive on Michigan Avenue, leading to his death, gets 9 years in prison
entries.summary: <p>A homeless man with a history of mental illness and violent behavior was sentenced to nine years in prison Friday for throwing the punch that led to a Michigan Avenue pedestrian’s death in 2023.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Judge Charles Burns said that despite evidence that Henry Graham suffers from severe schizophrenia, the “chilling” nature of the random attack requires a stiff sentence.</p><p>Graham, 52, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/25/murder-chicago-magnificent-mile-henry-graham-russell-long" target="_blank" ><u>found guilty</u></a> of involuntary manslaughter in a bench trial in June.</p><p>Though prosecutors had charged Graham with first-degree murder, Burns found him guilty of the lesser charge, siding with defense attorneys who’d argued that under Illinois case law Graham could not have expected a single punch to kill Russell Long, a 53-year-old vice president at Northern Trust Bank.</p><p>At the sentencing hearing, Burns said Graham, who has a long record of convictions for punching and kicking people and who has active court cases for allegedly attacking an Evanston police officer and destroying jail property, “has had a life full of violence.”</p><p>“It is a factor that I’m very concerned about, that society needs to be protected from Henry Graham," Burns said.</p><p>Graham, wearing a beige jail uniform, spent most of the hearing slumped in his chair, staring down at the defense table.</p><p>Asked by Burns if he had anything to say, Graham replied, “I really don’t have anything to say. I never thought that I’d be responsible for laying someone to rest.”</p><p>Later, when Burns asked him whether he wanted to appeal his conviction, Graham said, “For manslaughter? No.”</p><p>After talking to his attorney, he changed his answer to, “OK, yes.”</p><p>Long was out shopping on the day of the attack in June 2023, carrying a pair of new blue jeans in a shopping bag and walking south near 630 N. Michigan Ave.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1e0000" name="image-1e0000"></a> </div><p>Without warning, Graham zoomed up behind Long and punched him in the back of his head. Long pitched forward, hitting the sidewalk with his face.</p><p>Long suffered extensive head injuries, including facial and skull fractures and bleeding of his brain. He died 13 days later at Northwestern Memorial Hospital.</p><p>Immediately after the attack, witnesses pointed Graham out to Chicago police. Police say Graham admitted he hit Long but claimed it happened after Long bumped into him.</p><p>Officers released Graham.</p><p>Graham was accused of attacking other people in the following months, according to police reports.</p><p>Long’s death and Graham’s history were featured last year in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Sun-Times series</u></a>, “Failure to treat, failure to protect,” about downtown attacks by people with severe, untreated mental illness who cycle in and out of jails, prisons and hospitals.</p><p>Assistant Cook County State’s Attorney Sean Brady, who pushed for a 10-year prison sentence, read victim impact statements from Long’s older brother, Daniel Long, and Kristen Maurice, a longtime friend of Long.</p><p>Daniel Long wrote: “I cannot put into words how horrific his passing was.” He described his younger brother as “unrecognizable” in the intensive care unit.</p><p>“The last images of him will haunt me forever,” he wrote.</p><p>He added that Graham’s history was one of “basically assault and release, assault and release, assault and release – until somebody is killed.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-db0000" name="module-db0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" >Failure to Treat, Failure to Protect</a></h3>The Chicago Sun-Times followed the trial of Henry Graham in the 2023 death of Russell Long as part of its series focused on the failures of government and the mental health system in Chicago.<br><ul id="rte-d334ef12-7175-11f1-8fe9-c34205311ff9"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/22/mental-illness-murder-henry-graham-cook-county-court" >Man accused of killing bank executive on Mag Mile lacked ‘mental state’ to prove intent, his lawyer says</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/25/murder-chicago-magnificent-mile-henry-graham-russell-long" >Killer of Northern Trust bank executive convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2023 Mag Mile attack</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/04/10/mentally-ill-downtown-killings-chicago-police-department-mental-health-care" >For accused mentally ill killers and their victims, help comes too little too late</a></li></ul></div> </div><p>Maurice wrote about Russell Long’s kindness, intelligence, sense of humor and love of photography and music. “I still can’t go near Michigan Avenue, the street Russ and I walked countless times,” she wrote.</p><p>Assistant Public Defender Celeste Addyman asked Burns to consider that in Graham’s mind, Graham thought he had been provoked, which is why he threw the punch — an argument Burns found unpersuasive.</p><p>Tragedies like Long’s killing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/05/31/mentally-ill-illinois-general-assembly-downtown-killings-chicago-police-department-mental-health-care-susan-doig-failure-treat-protect" target="_blank" >prompted the General Assembly to pass a measure</a> to address the issue of mental illness in people charged with crimes.</p><p>The legislation, signed last year by the governor, set up a task force that on Friday approved recommendations to address how those people are evaluated and treated. Next week, the committee will vote on ways to pay for those recommendations.</p><p>The task force hopes to improve the process for determining if a defendant with mental illness can be treated outside jail as an “outpatient” or must wait in jail for a bed to open up in a state-operated mental health facility.</p><p>One aim is to keep people with brain disorders like Alzheimer’s disease out of state mental hospitals to make room for people who have serious psychiatric conditions and are charged with the most serious crimes.</p><p>The Sun-Times’ series found a persistent lack of state beds for defendants who judges say must be evaluated and treated to become mentally fit for trial.</p><p>The task force has members from the General Assembly, the courts, law enforcement and the mental health system. Under the law, it must deliver a report by Nov. 1.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" target="_blank" >Failure to treat, failure to protect — A Chicago Sun-Times series.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/04/11/mentally-ill-downtown-killings-chicago-mental-health-care-treatment-mark-heyrman" >Unprovoked killings in downtown Chicago show a need for more mental health resources</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/shavon-gayden-brett-balmer-chicago-crime" >Judge orders woman detained in killing of 7-year-old, saying she’s ‘as dangerous as a person can be’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
